sections.other:
Obesity triggers the accumulation of immune cells within adipose tissue, which subsequently promotes low-grade inflammation and disrupts insulin signaling . Initially, research focused on macrophages as the primary immune cells, yet recent studies have brought to light the involvement of other cell types, such as T and B lymphocytes (including their sub-classes), neutrophils, eosinophils, and natural killer cells . Within the altered environment of adipose tissues in obesity, these cell types undergo complex phenotypic changes, rendering them highly diverse. The excessive buildup of fat in adipocytes triggers heightened numbers and activity of M1 macrophages, neutrophils, natural killer cells, Th1 cells, Th17 cells, and B cells, while concurrently diminishing the presence of eosinophils, Th2 cells, and regulatory T cells , .

Mast cell accumulation has been detected in the white adipose tissue (WAT) of mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) . Similarly, individuals with obesity exhibit higher mast cell counts in both subcutaneous (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) compared to individuals with a BMI < 25 , . In addition, mast cells isolated from SAT in individuals with obesity show increased activation and release of inflammatory cytokines , indicating their potential involvement in adipose tissue inflammation. Notably, mast cells in human VAT tend to localize within fibrosis bundles and secrete tryptase, promoting fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis , , which suggests a possible role in adipose tissue fibrosis. Nevertheless, the functional consequences of increased mast cells in adipose tissue remain a topic of debate. Earlier studies using mast cell-deficient mice ( Kit W/W-v and Kit W-sh/W-sh , which lack mature mast cells due to a mutation in the c-Kit promoter region) and mast cell stabilizers (disodium cromoglycate and ketotifen) indicate that mast cell deficiency or inactivation protects against weight gain and insulin resistance induced by HFD , . These findings raise the possibility that targeting mast cells could be a therapeutic strategy for metabolic disorders. However, recent studies using Kit -independent mast cell-deficient mice ( Kit +/+ Cpa3 Cre/+ and Mcpt5- Cre+ R-DTA + ) has shown no discernible impact on the development of obesity and its associated conditions , . Similarly, in a mixed human cohort with or without obesity, mRNA levels of mast cell-associated tryptase ( TPSB2 ) in VAT show no correlation with insulin resistance parameters .

Activated mast cells release an array of mediators, including histamine, serotonin, prostaglandins (PGs), proteases, cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors, which hold the potential to influence nearby cells with both local and systemic effects. For instance, mast cells can sense colder temperatures and release histamine, triggering the expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in adipocytes . Conversely, serotonin suppresses UCP1 expression . Mast cell-derived 15-deoxy-delta PGJ 2 and PGD 2 contribute to adipogenesis and eosinophilic inflammation , respectively. Moreover, mast cells produce interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), which fosters M1 macrophage polarization , indicating an indirect contribution of mast cells to obesity and insulin resistance by influencing adipocytes and other immune cells within adipose tissue.

Sirtuin, a family of NAD + -dependent protein/histone deacetylases, ranging from Sirt1 to Sirt7, is evolutionarily conserved across species, from bacteria to mammals . Our previous study revealed that antigen-stimulated mast cells express selectively increased levels of Sirt6 . Genetic deletion of Sirt6 aggravates mast cell degranulation and anaphylactic responses, while overexpression or pharmacological activation of Sirt6 suppresses them , . However, the direct contribution of Sirt6 in mast cells to metabolic phenotypes in adipose tissue remains unclear.

In this study, we show that mice with mast cell-specific Sirt6 knockout (KO) exhibit increased inflammation and fibrosis in adipose tissue when fed a high-fat diet. This process is driven by mast cell-derived galectin-3. Notably, Sirt6 deficiency further promotes the expansion of a fibroinflammatory mast cell population ( Tpsab1 high , Cd44 high , and Nfkb1 high ), highlighting a mechanism by which mast cells contribute to adipose tissue inflammation and fibrosis.
sections.results:
We and other researchers have reported that Sirt6 expression in adipocytes and macrophages is lower in humans and mice with obesity compared to lean controls – . Therefore, we investigated whether Sirt6 is also repressed in mast cells within obese adipose tissue. Immunostaining of human omental adipose tissue sections confirmed that individuals with obesity (BMI ≥ 30) had a higher number of total and degranulated mast cells compared to individuals with a BMI < 25 (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ), consistent with the previous reports , . Western blotting revealed a significant decrease in Sirt6 protein levels in mast cells from individuals with obesity (Fig. ). Moreover, Sirt6 protein levels in mast cells from the omental fat depot were negatively correlated with BMI and plasma leptin levels, while plasma adiponectin levels remained unchanged (Fig. ). Reduced Sirt6 expression in mast cells under obese conditions was also observed in mice: Western blotting of mast cells isolated from epididymal adipose tissue (EAT) of 16-week-HFD-fed mice showed lower Sirt6 levels compared with lean mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Human and mouse ADMCs showed purities greater than 90% (Supplementary Fig. ). Since neither reached complete (100%) purity, we isolated ADMC and non-ADMC populations from SVF fractions and compared their mast cell marker gene expression, which demonstrated markedly higher expression of key functional genes in ADMCs (Supplementary Fig. ). We also confirmed that the numbers of total and degranulated mast cells in EAT were elevated in HFD-fed mice compared with lean mice (Fig. ).

Furthermore, we observed an age-dependent increase in the number of total and degranulated mast cells in EAT (Supplementary Fig. ), along with a reduction in Sirt6 protein levels in aged adipose-derived mast cells (ADMCs) (Supplementary Fig. ). Given that obese adipose tissue is exposed to a highly obesogenic inflammatory microenvironment, we hypothesized that free fatty acids, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and insulin may regulate Sirt6 expression in mast cells. Results indicate that treating bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) with palmitate or TNFα reduced Sirt6 protein levels, while insulin treatment had no effect (Supplementary Fig. ).

To evaluate the role of mast cell Sirt6 in obesity, we generated mast cell-specific Sirt6 KO ( Sirt6 fl/fl ; Cma1-Cre ) mice, by crossing Sirt6-floxed ( Sirt6 fl/fl ) mice with Cma1-Cre (also known as Mcpt5, which encodes mast cell protease-5) mice. Successful deletion of Sirt6 was confirmed by western blotting of ADMCs isolated from the stromal vascular fraction (SVF) of EAT (Supplementary Fig. ). Cma1-Cre mice, Sirt6 KO mice ( Sirt6 -/- ), and their wild-type (WT) littermates ( Sirt6 fl/fl ) were fed a 60% HFD or normal chow diet (NCD) for 16 weeks, starting at six weeks of age (Fig. ). Despite similar total food intake, KO mice showed higher body weight than WT mice on HFD (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). KO mice fed an NCD displayed slight impairment in glucose and insulin tolerance, while other metabolic parameters, except for BAT, remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. ). On an HFD, however, KO mice exhibited markedly impaired glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). No significant differences were observed between Cma1-Cre and WT mice.

To explore the mechanisms behind the greater weight gain in HFD-fed KO mice, we assessed caloric intake and energy expenditure using indirect calorimetry. KO mice showed reduced VO₂ and energy expenditure (EE) during the light cycle compared to WT mice, with VCO₂ also tending to decrease (Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, thermogenic responses in the inguinal adipose tissue (IAT) of KO mice were diminished (Supplementary Fig. ). Correspondingly, the wet weight of EAT and their adipocyte size were significantly increased in KO mice (Fig. ).

Since Sirt6 deficiency in mast cells could promote their infiltration into non-adipose tissues, we next examined liver phenotypes. KO mice exhibited increased liver wet weight, although liver weight normalized to body weight remained unchanged (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ), suggesting this increase reflects overall obesity rather than a liver-specific effect. Histological and biochemical analyses revealed elevated mast cell infiltration and increased hepatic fat accumulation in KO mice (Supplementary Fig. ). Together, these findings suggest that Sirt6 deficiency in mast cells may enhance their infiltration into adipose tissue and other metabolic organs in response to HFD feeding and contribute to metabolic dysfunction.

Since adipose tissue mast cells have been linked to obesity-related glucose intolerance and inflammation , we evaluated the accumulation of mast cells and other inflammatory cells in adipose tissue. Toluidine blue staining of adipose tissue sections revealed significantly increased both total and degranulated mast cell numbers in EAT and IAT in KO mice compared to WT (Fig. ). KO mast cells also exhibited elevated expression of marker genes associated with mast cell activation (e.g., Kit and Cpa3 encoding carboxypeptidase A3) and degranulation (e.g., Tpsab1 encoding tryptase alpha/beta 1) (Fig. ).

The Olefsky group previously identified LTB 4 as a potent chemokine for immune cells in obese mice , . In line with these findings, we observed higher levels of LTB 4 in the adipocyte fraction compared to the SVF following 16 weeks of HFD feeding (Supplementary Fig. ). To investigate the potential role of LTB 4 in mast cell chemotaxis into adipose tissues, we conducted migration assays using LTB 4 as a chemoattractant. We confirmed that Sirt6-deficient mast cells exhibited significantly higher expression of Ltb4r1 , the gene encoding the LTB 4 receptor, while mRNA levels of other eicosanoid receptors were unchanged (Supplementary Fig. ). We then placed BMMCs on a transwell insert and measured their migration in response to LTB 4 in the lower chamber (Supplementary Fig. ). LTB 4 significantly promoted BMMC migration, and this effect was further amplified in Sirt6-deficient cells. Notably, treatment with CP-105696, a selective LTB 4 receptor antagonist, effectively abolished the chemotactic response of BMMCs to adipocyte-conditioned medium (Supplementary Fig. ). These findings suggest that adipocyte-derived LTB 4 acts as a potent chemoattractant by binding to its receptor on mast cells, thereby promoting their migration into tissues.

To obtain in-depth evidence of Sirt6 regulation of mast cells, we conducted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on SVF from the EAT of WT and KO mice after 16 weeks of HFD feeding. In total, 19,878 cells from WT mice ( n = 2, pooled) and 33,983 cells from KO mice ( n = 3, pooled) were analyzed. We identified 13 distinct clusters within the SVF, characterizing each based on the most enriched genes using cell type-specific markers from the literature , . These clusters included adipose-derived stem and progenitor cells (ASPCs, marked by Pdfgra and Dpep1 ), macrophages (Mφ, marked by Adgre1 and Ms4a7 ), and mast cells (marked by Cpa3 and Cma1 ) (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Cells from both WT and KO SVF samples appeared in all identified clusters, suggesting that each cell type corresponded to a shared cell lineage (Supplementary Fig. ). Frequency analysis showed an increased proportion of mast cells in KO SVF samples, with proportions of other cell populations remaining unchanged (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ).

A comparison of mast cells from WT and KO mice revealed significant differences in transcriptional states: KO mast cells had elevated expression of genes associated with mast cell activation and degranulation (Fig. ). Gene ontology analysis further indicated that KO mast cells were enriched in transcripts linked to mast cell activation and degranulation (Fig. ).

In addition to the increased accumulation of mast cells in KO mice, F4/80 immunostaining and flow cytometry revealed a significant rise in the number of macrophages, particularly M1-type macrophages, and crown-like structures (CLSs) in the EAT of KO mice fed a HFD for 16 weeks, compared to WT mice (Supplementary Fig. ). This was further supported by qPCR analysis, which showed significantly elevated mRNA levels of macrophage markers ( Adgre1 and Itgam ) and M1 type macrophage markers ( Il6 , Il1b , Ccl2 , Ccr2 , and Nos2 ) in the EATs of KO mice relative to those of WT mice (Supplementary Fig. ). To gain a deeper understanding of cellular heterogeneity, adipose tissue macrophages were deconstructed from the remaining scRNA-seq data and reclustered. This analysis identified three distinct subpopulations: Lpl -enriched lipid-associated macrophages (LAM), Cbr2 -enriched non-perivascular-like macrophages (NPVM), and Lyve1 -enriched perivascular-like macrophages (PVM), consistent with previous observation (Supplementary Fig. ). A comparison of these macrophage subpopulations revealed a significant increase in the relative expression of obesity-enriched genes and a significant decrease in lean-enriched genes due to mast cell Sirt6 deficiency (Supplementary Fig. ).

Since both mast cells and macrophages in adipose tissue develop more pro-inflammatory characteristics in Sirt6 KO mice, we questioned which cell type might initially trigger their infiltration into the tissue. To explore this, we analyzed immune cell dynamics in mice after 2 weeks of HFD feeding (Supplementary Fig. ). At this early time point, there were no significant differences in body weight, wet weight of fat tissues and liver, or adipocyte size in the EAT of WT and KO mice (Supplementary Fig. ). However, histological and qPCR analyses of EAT showed that mast cell numbers and their marker genes were significantly elevated in KO mice compared to WT mice (Supplementary Fig. ). In contrast, macrophage infiltration—assessed by F4/80 immunofluorescence and qPCR—as well as T cell and eosinophil markers by qPCR, showed no significant differences between genotypes (Supplementary Fig. ). These patterns persisted through 5 weeks of HFD feeding (Supplementary Fig. ), suggesting that mast cell activation likely precedes the recruitment of macrophages, T cells and eosinophils during the early stages of HFD-induced adipose tissue inflammation.

To further investigate the role of mast cells in promoting macrophage activation in adipose tissue, we conducted in vitro experiments. ADMCs were isolated from the SVF of EAT from WT or KO mice fed an NCD and cultured for 48 h to collect mast cell conditioned media (MC-CM), which was then incubated with bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs) prepared as previously described . qPCR results showed that incubation with MC-CM increased the mRNA level of chemokine and cytokines such as Tnfa , Il6 , and Ccl2 in BMMs, with an even greater increase with MC-CM from Sirt6 KO mast cells (Supplementary Fig. ). These in vitro findings, together with in vivo observations from the shorter HFD studies (Supplementary Figs. , ), suggest that mast cell Sirt6 plays a role in macrophage activation and chemotaxis.

Since mast cells release signals that attract fibroblasts and influence tissue fibrosis in adipose tissue and other connective tissues , , we next investigated the impact of mast cell Sirt6 deficiency on adipose tissue fibrosis. Gene expression profiling categorized three SVF subpopulations: DPP4 + stem cells, ICAM1 + progenitor cells, and COL1A1 high pro-fibrotic cells. Mast cell Sirt6 deficiency led to a decreased stem cell population and an increased proportion of pro-fibrotic cells (Fig. ). Fibrosis-related genes, such as Col1a1 , Timp1 , and Sdc1 , were significantly upregulated in SVFs from KO mice (Fig. ). Human Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) analysis of VAT and SAT also revealed a positive correlation between the mast cell marker gene CPA3 and fibrosis-related genes like COL6A1 , COL1A1 , TGFB1 , TIMP2 , and COL3A1 (Supplementary Fig. ).

In line with the transcriptome data, mast cell Sirt6 deficiency led to an increase in Sirius Red positive areas and hydroxyproline content in EAT (Fig. ). qPCR analysis further confirmed the elevated expression of fibrosis-related genes in the EAT of KO mice (Fig. ). To directly demonstrate crosstalk between mast cells and fibroblasts (or their precursors), we conducted in vitro experiments in which ASPCs were cocultured with ADMCs isolated from WT or Sirt6 KO mice. Fibrosis-related genes were elevated in ASPCs incubated with Sirt6-deficient mast cells compared to controls (Fig. ).

To investigate the causal role of mast cell Sirt6 in maintaining systemic metabolic homeostasis, we transplanted either WT or Sirt6-deficient mast cells into mast cell-deficient Kit W-sh/W-sh mice and fed them a HFD for 14 weeks (Fig. ). Successful reconstitution of mast cells in the Kit W-sh/W-sh recipient mice was confirmed by flow cytometric analysis of SVF from EAT for FcɛRI + CD117 + cells, showing 1.74% vs. 2.91% of total SVF in mice reconstituted with mast cells from WT and KO mice, respectively (Supplementary Fig. ). Consequently, mice receiving Sirt6-deficient mast cells demonstrated significant increases in body weight gain, white fat pad mass, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance compared to mice reconstituted with WT mast cells (Fig. ). Histological, flow cytometric, and qPCR analyses revealed larger adipocytes, a higher number of total and degranulated mast cells, and increased macrophage infiltration, especially M1-type macrophages, in mice transplanted with Sirt6-deficient mast cells (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). These results suggest that mast cell Sirt6 is essential for the metabolic protection seen in Kit W-sh/W-sh mice on an HFD.

Although we conclude that Sirt6-deficient mast cells affect adipose tissue macrophages, leading to tissue inflammation and systemic glucose intolerance, we further investigated how the adipose immune cell landscape has changed. We analyzed scRNA-seq data, focusing exclusively on hematopoietic cells. Using known cell-type markers, we identified distinct clusters, including macrophages, T cells, B cells (both plasma and tissue-resident), neutrophils, natural killer (NK) cells, dendritic cells (DC), proliferating cells, Th17 cells, and mast cells (Supplementary Fig. ). A comparison of WT and KO cells showed moderate differences in overall cellular composition. Notably, cell-cell communication analysis indicated that mast cells, acting as signal-sending cells, exhibited the most significant variability due to Sirt6 deficiency (Supplementary Fig. ). Analysis of ligand-receptor pairs suggested that mast cell signals primarily target monocytes and macrophages, with fewer interactions with other cell types (Supplementary Fig. ). This indicates that macrophages are the main effector cells influenced by Sirt6-deficient mast cells in promoting adipose tissue inflammation and fibrosis.

To identify pathways in mast cells that may contribute to macrophage activation, we conducted communication probability analysis. Among the affected pathways, galectin-3 and galectin-9 signaling were commonly upregulated in KO mice (Supplementary Fig. ), coinciding with increased expression of galectin-3 and galectin-9 (encoded by Lgals3 and Lgals9 , respectively) in KO mast cells (Supplementary Fig. ). While macrophages and other immune cells, such as dendritic cells and neutrophils, are known to express high levels of galectin-3 – , no difference in expression was observed between genotypes (Supplementary Fig. ). Along with elevated mRNA, protein levels of galectin-3 and galectin-9 in the blood and EAT of KO mice were also increased (Fig. ). In addition, mast cell-derived galectin signaling toward monocytes and macrophages was heightened in KO mice, as demonstrated by ligand-receptor signaling analysis (Fig. ).

To validate these findings, we examined whether and how Sirt6 regulates Lgals3 and Lgals9 expression in mast cells by transfecting mast cells with siRNA targeting Sirt6. Sirt6 depletion led to increased mRNA levels of Lgals3 and Lgals9 in mast cells (Fig. ). Given that NF-κB binds to specific κB response elements in the Lgals3 promoter to drive its transcription , we assessed whether NF-κB binding at the Lgals3 and Lgals9 promoters was affected by Sirt6 deficiency. ChIP assays showed that NF-κB was normally enriched at these promoters in control cells, with a notable increase in NF-κB binding at the Lgals3 promoter following Sirt6 silencing (Fig. ). Since Sirt6 is known to regulate gene transcription through histone deacetylase activity, especially at H3K9 and H3K56 near NF-κB target genes ,, , we further examined Sirt6 enrichment at the Lgals3 and Lgals9 promoters. ChIP assays indicated that Sirt6 was typically enriched at these promoters in control cells, but this was reduced in Sirt6-silenced cells (Fig. ). Moreover, Ac-H3K9 occupancy at the Lgals3 and Lgals9 promoters significantly increased in Sirt6-silenced cells (Fig. ), aligning with the higher H3K9 acetylation observed in these cells (Fig. ).

To evaluate the relevance of these findings in humans, we examined the association between Sirt6 and galectin-3 or galectin-9. Consistent with previous studies , , individuals with obesity exhibited elevated circulating levels of galectin-3 (Fig. ). Interestingly, galectin-3 levels were inversely correlated with mast cell Sirt6 protein levels (Fig. ), suggesting that mast cell Sirt6 may inhibit circulating galectin-3 concentrations in obesity. While galectin-9 levels were also elevated in individuals with obesity, they did not show a significant correlation with mast cell Sirt6 levels (Fig. ). In addition, galectin-3 expression was higher in ADMCs from subjects with obesity, aged mice, HFD-fed mice as well as in the EAT and ADMC-conditioned media (ADMC-CM) of Sirt6 KO mice compared to their respective controls (Supplementary Fig. ).

Given that mast cell Sirt6 deficiency promotes fibro-inflammatory features, we isolated mast cells and further divided them into two subclusters, MC1 and MC2 (Fig. ). In MC2 subcluster, 600 genes were upregulated, while 278 genes were downregulated compared to MC1 cells (Fig. ). Transcription factor enrichment analysis (ChEA) and KEGG pathway analysis revealed that inflammation and fibrosis signaling pathways were enriched in MC2 cells relative to MC1 cells (Fig. ). Specifically, mast cell marker genes ( Tpsab1 , Cpa3 , and Tpsab2 ) as well as genes associated with inflammation ( Nfkb1 , Il6 , and Ccl3 ) and fibrosis ( Cd44 , Lgals3 , and Lgals9 ) were significantly upregulated in MC2 cells (Fig. ).

GTEx analysis of human VAT and SAT indicated a positive correlation between galectin-3 or galectin-9 and fibrosis-associated genes (Supplementary Fig. ). Further, we analyzed the heterogeneity of human adipose tissue mast cells (hMCs) using publicly available single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq datasets . Our analysis identified two distinct subpopulations of hMCs: hMC1, characterized by the expression of MT-ND3 , MT-CO3 , FABP4 , and CD36 ; and hMC2, marked by NFKB1 , LGALS3 , TPSAB1 , and CD44 (Supplementary Fig. ). Notably, the expression of hMC2 marker genes was also positively correlated with BMI (Supplementary Fig. ), suggesting that in individuals with obesity, mast cells might shift towards a fibroinflammatory phenotype, which could contribute to adipose tissue fibroinflammation.

Our experimental results support the idea that Sirt6 deficiency in mast cells leads to inflammation and fibrosis in adipose tissue, mediated by the upregulated action of galectin-3 or galectin-9 on macrophages and fibroblasts. To establish a causal relationship between Sirt6 and galectin-3 or galectin-9, we conducted an additional adoptive transfer study in which Kit W-sh/W-sh recipient mice received either WT or Sirt6 KO mast cells transduced with lentivirus carrying shRNAs targeting galectin-3 or galectin-9. These mice were subsequently placed on an HFD for 14 weeks (Fig. ). Successful knockdown of galectin-3 or galectin-9 in the mast cells, as well as its sustained suppression throughout the long-term HFD feeding period, was confirmed by western blotting and immunofluorescence staining (Supplementary Fig. ). As previously shown (Fig. ), transferring Sirt6-deficient mast cells alone led to increased body weight gain, glucose and insulin intolerance, adipocyte hypertrophy, and fibroinflammation in EAT, compared to mice receiving WT mast cells (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Notably, the transfer of mast cells deficient in both Sirt6 and galectin-3 reversed most of the metabolic disturbances in Kit W-sh/W-sh mice with Sirt6-deficient mast cells, except for total number of mast cells in EAT.

The role of mast cell-derived galectin-3 in macrophage chemotaxis and M1 polarization was examined. GB1211, an extracellular galectin-3 inhibitor, reduced macrophage migration but not M1 polarization (Supplementary Fig. ). In contrast, galectin-3 knockdown in mast cells suppressed M1 polarization (Supplementary Fig. ). These findings suggest extracellular galectin-3 is key for macrophage recruitment, while intracellular galectin-3 promotes M1 polarization via an unknown mechanism. This aligns with galectins functioning as both secretory and intracellular proteins—synthesized on endoplasmic reticulum-bound and free ribosomes—and involved in vesicle trafficking, cell growth, apoptosis, and immune responses . The adoptive transfer of mast cells deficient in both Sirt6 and galectin-9 only partially reversed the phenotypes of mice carrying Sirt6 KO mast cells (Supplementary Fig. ). Collectively, these findings strongly suggest that galectin-3 in Sirt6-deficient mast cells plays a key role in driving inflammation and fibrosis in adipose tissue following HFD feeding.
sections.discussion:
In this study, we identified an obesity- and age-related decline in Sirt6 expression in mast cells within adipose tissue, uncovering a novel role for Sirt6 in mast cell–mediated fibroinflammatory remodeling during metabolic stress and possibly aging. Sirt6 is a well-established regulator of metabolic and inflammatory pathways in adipose tissue, predominantly expressed in adipocytes and, to a lesser extent, in immune cells of the stromal vascular fraction. Its expression, controlled by multiple transcription factors and microRNAs, declines with age and obesity in both mice and humans – , a process further worsened by age-related reductions in NAD⁺, which impair its enzymatic activity . We previously showed that Sirt6 in adipocytes and macrophages promotes M2 macrophage polarization while suppressing the M1 phenotype , and that Sirt6 in eosinophils supports thermogenesis . Here, we demonstrate that mast cell Sirt6 protects against mast cell activation and thereby limits macrophage infiltration, inflammation, and fibrosis in adipose tissue, consistent with its coordinated role in other adipose-resident cells. Mast cell–specific deletion of Sirt6 led to increased mast cell accumulation and degranulation, aggravating adipose inflammation and fibrosis in obese mice, partly via galectin-3 as a downstream effector (Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, Sirt6 deficiency in mast cells reduced thermogenic gene expression and energy expenditure, indicating impaired systemic energy homeostasis. While the precise mechanisms remain to be clarified, our findings highlight a central role for mast cell Sirt6 in regulating both local fibroinflammatory responses and whole-body metabolism.

Although macrophages are the most studied immune cells in adipose tissue inflammation and obesity, with mast cells receiving less attention, our findings reveal that mast cells play a significant role in macrophage infiltration and polarization. Comparing the infiltration of mast cells and macrophages under short- and long-term HFD feeding revealed that mast cells activate earlier than macrophages. This early activation suggests that mast cells may play a role in recruiting macrophages and driving adipose inflammation. The current CellChat results confirm that mast cell signaling predominantly affects macrophages, suggesting a stepwise immune response in adipose tissue during obesity.

Further analysis revealed that Sirt6 deficiency in mast cells leads to elevated secretion of multiple galectins, including galectin-1, galectin-3, and galectin-9. Among these, galectin-3 emerged as the predominant and functionally relevant mediator of fibroinflammation. In HFD-fed wild-type mice, galectin-3 levels in adipose tissue–resident mast cells were elevated compared to NCD-fed controls, and this increase was further amplified in Sirt6 KO mice. Concordantly, circulating galectin-3 levels were also higher in these mice, indicating both local and systemic effects. In human visceral adipose tissue, mast cells exhibited an inverse correlation between SIRT6 and LGALS3 expression, suggesting a conserved regulatory axis across species. Our in vitro assays demonstrated that galectin-3 secreted by Sirt6-deficient mast cells promotes macrophage chemotaxis, an effect that was significantly blunted by a galectin-3–specific inhibitor, highlighting galectin-3 as a key mast cell–derived chemoattractant. In vivo, the functional importance of galectin-3 was confirmed by adoptive transfer experiments: transplantation of mast cells deficient in both Sirt6 and galectin-3 into mast cell–deficient mice significantly attenuated adipose tissue fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and systemic glucose intolerance, compared to transfer of Sirt6-deficient mast cells alone. In contrast, transplantation of mast cells lacking both Sirt6 and galectin-9 led to only partial improvement in these parameters. Although galectin-1 levels were similarly increased in Sirt6-deficient mast cells, previous studies have highlighted its predominantly immunoregulatory and anti-inflammatory roles in various contexts .

It is noteworthy that our data clearly show galectin-3 is abundantly expressed in adipose tissue mast cells lacking Sirt6 and correlates with its plasma levels, although previous studies indicating that macrophages are the primary source of systemic galectin-3 . Galectin-3 is a beta-galactoside-binding lectin with IgE-binding properties . It has been shown to mediate immune cell chemotaxis and inflammation, but the results are inconsistent. Galectin-3-deficient mice have reduced atherogenesis and fewer perivascular inflammatory infiltrates and mast cells . However, studies have shown that galectin-3 in mast cells can either suppress antigen-induced chemotaxis or lead to impaired mediator release upon IgE stimulation .

Conditioned medium from Sirt6-deficient mast cells promoted both macrophage chemotaxis and M1 polarization. While chemotaxis was suppressed by both galectin-3 inhibition and knockdown, M1 polarization was only reduced by galectin-3 knockdown. Given that galectins function both extracellularly and intracellularly , these findings suggest that extracellular galectin-3 mediates macrophage recruitment, whereas intracellular galectin-3 may drive M1 polarization via an unknown mechanism. Moreover, the upregulation of classical chemokines in Sirt6-deficient mast cells likely contributes to enhanced macrophage chemotaxis. Collectively, these results indicate that Sirt6 regulates mast cell–driven macrophage recruitment and activation through coordinated control of inflammatory genes, chemokines, and galectin-3.

Mast cell-derived mediators contributing to adipose tissue fibrosis have been previously investigated. For instance, mast cells can promote fibrotic remodeling through the secretion of TGFβ and IL-4—cytokines that are also produced by M2 macrophages and implicated in adipose fibrosis . In our study, Sirt6 KO mice displayed increased adipose fibrosis and M1 macrophages, but not M2 macrophages, suggesting mast cells are central to fibrosis regulation in adipose tissue. scRNA-seq analysis on SVF revealed two distinct mast cell subpopulations, MC1 and MC2. MC1 cells, found in both WT and KO mice, express classic mast cell markers like Cpa3 , Tpsab1 , and Tpsab2 , consistent with a traditional mast cell profile. In contrast, MC2 cells, while also expressing these markers, show significantly higher levels in KO mice compared to WT. These MC2 cells exhibit elevated expression of pro-inflammatory genes ( Nfκb1 , Il6 , and Ccl3 ) and fibrosis-associated genes ( Cd44 , Lgals3 , and Lgals9 ). Galectin-3 is widely recognized as a pro-fibrotic mediator due to its role in promoting inflammation and collagen VI production in the extracellular matrix , , despite some contradictory findings . Our results from mast cell reconstitution model in Kit W-sh/W-sh mice showed that galectin-3 from mast cells is closely associated with adipose tissue fibrosis in obese mice. We and others show that plasma galectin-3 levels were higher in individuals with obesity compared to individuals with a BMI < 25. Analysis of public human data revealed a significant correlation between fibrosis gene expression and galectin-3 levels in visceral and subcutaneous fat, suggesting a role for galectin-3 in adipose tissue fibrosis. Further investigation into galectin-3’s molecular role in adipocyte fibrosis in obesity could provide deeper insights into adipose tissue biology.

Notably, the elevated expression of CD44, a hyaluronan receptor, in MC2 cells is of interest. Given the well-established role of hyaluronan-CD44 interactions in fibrosis in organs like the liver, kidney, and heart – , it is plausible that hyaluronan binding to CD44 on mast cells could initiate the release of fibrogenic mediators, driving fibrotic changes.

While our findings underscore mast cell Sirt6’s role in adipose inflammation and fibrosis regulation, some limitations exist. First, we used Kit W-sh/W-sh mice for adoptive transfer experiments, yet Kit -independent mast cell-deficient models may be more suitable. Second, BMMCs are considered the gold standard for adoptive transfer as they can be expanded in vitro into a homogeneous, high-yield population, although they lack tissue-specific traits . In contrast, ADMCs retain an obesity-associated, metabolically primed phenotype, yet their limited yield and heterogeneity pose challenges for large-scale use . Nonetheless, ADMC-based transfer enables investigation of adipose-resident mast cell functions in a physiologically relevant context, and optimizing ex vivo expansion protocols may improve feasibility. Third, further exploration of triggers for mast cell degranulation in obese adipose tissue is needed. Elevated IgE levels in obesity suggest that IgE could activate mast cells , or non-IgE pathways like cholesterol or TLR ligands could stimulate mast cells , . Forth, we acknowledge the discrepancy in macrophage numbers observed between scRNA-seq data and results from flow cytometry and histological analyses. This difference likely arises because scRNA-seq can underestimate macrophage abundance due to incomplete dissociation of macrophages from adipocytes during tissue processing—an issue particularly pronounced in obese adipose tissue . Consequently, scRNA-seq is more appropriate for characterizing macrophage transcriptional profiles than for accurately quantifying their abundance. Fifth, Sirt6 deficiency in mast cells may promote their infiltration into other tissues—such as the liver and skeletal muscle—beyond adipose tissue. This may lead to systemic inflammation via the release of hepatokines, myokines, and other cytokines. Indeed, we observed increased mast cell accumulation in the livers of HFD-fed Sirt6 KO mice. Therefore, future studies are needed to determine the potential role of these inflammatory mediators from non-adipose tissues in contributing to the metabolic phenotypes observed. Lastly, there is a need for more comprehensive characterization of MC2 cells. While we have defined MC2 cells as Tpsab1 high , Cd44 high , and Nfkb1 high , in vivo models are lacking to show whether MC2 cells specifically regulate adipose tissue fibroinflammation. In addition, we were unable to validate the functional role of MC2 cells by transferring them into Kit W-sh/W-sh mice.

In conclusion, this study identifies mast cell Sirt6 as a key regulator of adipose fibroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction through galectin-3, providing mechanistic insight into mast cell contributions to adipose biology and pointing to potential therapeutic targets for obesity-related complications.
sections.methods:
Mast cell-deficient Kit W-sh/W-sh mice of the C57BL/6 background were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA). Mast cell-specific Sirt6 knockout mice ( Sirt6 fl/fl ; Cma1-Cre ) were generated as described previously .

Six-week-old male Sirt6 KO mice and WT littermates were provided either an NCD (SAM #31, Samtako, Osan, Korea) or a 60% HFD (#D12492, Research Diets, New Brunswick, NJ, USA) ad libitum for a duration of 2, 5, or 16 weeks. Food intake and body weight were monitored weekly throughout the study, and mice with abnormal body weights, typically exceeding 5 standard deviations, were excluded from the experiments.

Intraperitoneal glucose tolerance (1 g/kg of body weight) and intraperitoneal insulin tolerance tests (0.5 μ/kg of body weight) were conducted on mice after a 6-hour fast. Tail vein blood glucose levels were measured using a handheld glucometer (Roche Diagnostic, Indianapolis, IN, USA) at baseline and at 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min after the glucose challenge. Data were subsequently graphed as baseline-corrected areas under the curve (AUC).

For adoptive transfer experiments, FcεRI + CD117 + SVFs (2 × 10 6 ), freshly isolated from EAT of WT and KO mice or lentivirally transduced, were injected via the tail vein into 6-week-old Kit W-sh/W-sh mice that had been on an HFD for two weeks. Fourteen weeks after HFD feeding, mast cell reconstitution in the recipient mice was confirmed by flow cytometry and immunohistochemical staining for tryptase in adipose tissue sections.

All mice were housed in a controlled barrier facility with a 12-hour light/dark cycle and 60-70% humidity. This study protocol was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Jeonbuk National University (Permit No: JBNU-2020-0158).

We obtained omental fat tissues located near the gallbladder from patients who underwent elective or emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy at the Surgery Unit of Jeonbuk National University Hospital (Jeonju, Korea) between April 2022 and October 2022 and December 2023 and August 2024. The tissues were rinsed with PBS and immediately processed without snap frozen. Supplementary Table provides an overview of the demographic and clinical profiles of the 45 individuals who participated in this study. All patients provided written informed consent, and the study received approval from the Institutional Review Board of Jeonbuk National University Hospital (Permit No: JUH 2022-04-033).

Plasma levels of various analytes were determined using specific kits as per the manufacturer’s instructions. The following parameters were measured: insulin (#80-INSMS-E01 for human and #80-INSMS-E01 for mouse, ALPCO, Salem, NH, USA), leptin (#11-LEPHU-E01, ALPCO), adiponectin (#80-ADPHU-E01 for human and #47-ADPHUT-E01 for mouse, ALPCO), LTB 4 (#502390, Cayman, Michigan, USA), galectin-1 (#ab253212, Abcam, Cambridge, UK), galectin-3 (#BMS279-4 for human and #EMLGALS3 for mouse, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), and galectin-9 (#EH206RB for human and #EM33RB for mouse, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Liver and serum TG levels were determined using a TG assay kit (#AM157S-K, Asan Pharmaceutical, Seoul, Korea). To quantify liver TG, liver tissues (100 mg) were homogenized and extracted in a 1 ml mixture of 5% Triton X-100 in PBS. Hydroxyproline content in adipose tissue was assessed using a hydroxyproline assay kit (#QZBHYPRO1, Quickzyme Biosciences, Leiden, Netherlands).

Mice were housed in the Oxymax/CLAMS metabolic cage system from Columbus Instruments (Columbus, OH, USA), with one mouse per chamber. To avoid stress during analysis and allow adaptation, the mice were placed in the metabolic cages for one day. After 24 h of acclimatization, the mice were continuously monitored for 48 h under ad libitum feeding in a room set at 20–23 °C, with a 12 h light-dark cycle (6:00 pm to 6:00 am). The respiratory exchange ratio (VO 2 /VCO 2 ) was measured using the Oxymax system. Data collected during the 48 h of the experiment were used for analysis.

Tissues were fixed with 10% formalin and embedded in paraffin. Fixed tissues were cut into 6 μm sections and deparaffinized. Sections were stained with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) to assess adipocyte area and crown-like structures (at 200 × magnification) or toluidine blue to evaluate mast cell infiltration (at 200 ×, 400 ×, and 1000 × magnification). Quantification of adipocyte area, crown-like structures, and mast cell infiltration was performed by counting them in three distinct fields, with analysis done by an independent observer. Sirius Red staining was carried out on paraffin sections using saturated picric acid containing 0.1% DirectRed 80, and the results were expressed as a percentage of stained area. The stained areas were quantified using iSolution DT36 software (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) following established protocols . For immunofluorescence staining, tissue sections were labeled with antibodies against CD117 (ACK2, #14-1172-82, Thermo Fisher Scientific), FcεRI (#sc-390222, Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA), Sirt6 (#ab62739, Abcam), F4/80 (#ab6640, Abcam), Plin1 (#70R-1297, Fitzgerald, Concord, MA, USA), or tryptase (#sc-33676, Santa Cruz Biotechnology). After washing with PBS, sections were incubated with secondary antibodies, including Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (#A11032), Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (#A11012), Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (#A11008; all from Thermo Fisher Scientific), or DyLight 488-conjugated goat anti-rat IgG (#A110-105D2; Bethyl Laboratories, Montgomery, TX, USA). Sections were subsequently counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI).

Adipose-derived mast cells were obtained following previously described methods with minor modifications . Epididymal fat pads were dissected from 16-week-old male WT and KO mice that had been fed a HFD (60% kcal fat) for 10 weeks, rinsed three times in Krebs-Ringer (KR) buffer (119 mM NaCl, 4.74 mM KCl, 1.19 mM KH 2 PO4, 1.19 mM MgSO 4 ·7H 2 O, 20 mM NaHCO 3 , 10 mM HEPES, 2.54 mM CaCl 2 ·2H 2 O, pH 7.4), and homogenized in KR buffer containing 0.1% type I collagenase (# LS004194 , Worthington, Lakewood, NJ, USA). The tissues were shaken for 1 h at 37 °C, passed through a 100 μm filter, and centrifuged at 200 × g for 5 min. The resulting SVFs were incubated in ACK lysis buffer (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) for 3 min, followed by another centrifugation at 200 × g for 5 min, then resuspended in KR buffer. The FcεRI + CD117 + cells were isolated from SVFs using a human and mouse CD117 microbead kit instructions (#130-091-332 for human and #130-091-224 for mouse, Miltenyi Biotec, Waltham, MA, USA). To obtain a sufficient number of ADMCs for adoptive transfer, cells from ≥10 donor mice (each yielding ~ 2 g of EAT) were pooled for transfer into a single recipient mouse. The purity of the sorted FcεRI⁺CD117⁺ population was assessed through complementary approaches, including flow cytometry with a FACS Aria III (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) and immunofluorescence staining of cytospin preparations with mast cell markers (CD117 and FcεRI). These analyses demonstrated > 90% purity. The sorted FcεRI⁺CD117⁺ cells were then cultured for 3 days in medium supplemented with stem cell factor (SCF, 20 ng/ml), after which 2 × 10 6 cells were prepared for adoptive transfer into a single mouse.

Adipose stem and progenitor cells were isolated from EAT using the protocol established by Kilroy et al. . Briefly, the tissue was digested with collagenase, and the adherent fraction of the SVF was cultured. Cells were expanded to passage 2 and maintained in standard growth medium (DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS) until reaching 80–90% confluence. To confirm the identity of the stromal cell population, FACS was conducted using an APC-conjugated anti-PDGFRα antibody (#17-1401-81, eBioscience, San Diego, CA, USA). For fibrogenic differentiation, ASPCs were co-cultured with adipocyte CM–primed ADMCs. After three days of induction, cells were harvested for qPCR analysis of fibrosis-related gene expression.

scRNA-seq was performed using SVF cells isolated from EAT. Cell viability and concentration were assessed with the LUNA-FL™ Automated Fluorescence Cell Counter (Logos Biosystems, Anyang, Korea), following the 10 × Genomics Cell Preparation Guide (CG00053) and the Guidelines for Optimal Sample Preparation ( CG000126 ). Libraries were generated using the Chromium Controller and the 10 × Genomics Next GEM Single Cell 3’ v3.1 kit ( CG000315 ), with approximately 10,000 cells loaded per sample. Following droplet-based barcoding and reverse transcription, cDNA was amplified, end-repaired, A-tailed, and ligated to sequencing adapters. Final libraries were purified, quantified using qPCR (KAPA), and assessed for quality using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Sequencing was carried out on the Illumina HiSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) following the recommended read length parameters.

Raw reads were mapped to the mouse reference genome (GRCm38), with demultiplexing, alignment, and assignment of barcodes and unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) conducted using Cell Ranger software (v7.0.1). The data were imported into R (v4.3.2) and processed following the standard Seurat workflows (v5.0.1) . To filter out low-quality cells, we excluded those with > 20% of UMIs assigned to mitochondrial genes, those with < 1000 detected genes, and those with > 100,000 UMI counts. Genes not expressed in at least three cells were also excluded. Gene expression was normalized using a global-scaling normalization method (default options), and the 2000 most variable genes were selected and scaled. The top 30 principal components were utilized for clustering at a resolution of 0.8, employing the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions in Seurat. Cluster markers were identified using the FindAllMarkers function with default parameters, and clusters were manually annotated based on the expression of known markers, leveraging PanglaoDB and a recent published adipose tissue single-nucleus data . Doublets in the dataset were identified using the scDblFinder package (v1.14.0) with default parameters. Cells were visualized in a two-dimensional UMAP plot using the RunUMAP function. After cell type annotation, cell subpopulation annotation was performed. Then, low-quality clusters and doublet clusters were removed at a cluster level. One WT adipose tissue sample mixed with sperm (Cox8c + and Fabp9 + ) was excluded from further analysis. Subsequently, the data were re-analyzed using the aforementioned standard Seurat workflows.

For cell-cell communication analysis, CellChat (v1.6.1) was employed . The total number of interactions and interaction strengths, and communication probabilities for each cell signaling pathway were calculated using the computeCommunProbPathway function.

A publicly available human adipose tissue dataset was re-analyzed . Following the extraction of the CPA3 + mast cell cluster, normalization and scaling were performed. Single-cell RNA-seq and single-nucleus data were corrected using Harmony (v1.2.0) . The MC2 score was determined based on the expression levels of the top 40 DEGs of the MC2 subpopulation compared to the MC2 subpopulation. Gene ontology enrichment analysis was conducted using the EnrichR database .

3T3-L1 fibroblasts (#CL-173) and L929 fibroblasts (#CCL-1) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA, USA). To prepare adipocyte CM, 3T3-L1 fibroblasts were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS. Once confluent, the cells were treated with differentiation medium [MDI: DMEM, 10% FBS, 1 μM dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), 10 μg/ml insulin (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN, USA), and 0.5 mM isobutylmethylxanthine (Sigma-Aldrich)] for 2 days. The medium was then replaced with DMEM containing 10 μg/ml insulin for another 2 days, followed by 2 days in DMEM without insulin. Adipocyte CM was collected on day 6 after initial exposure to the differentiation medium.

Bone marrow cells were obtained by flushing bone marrow from the femurs and tibias of mice and cultured in α-MEM supplemented with 10% FBS. Macrophages were differentiated from bone marrow cells by culturing them in α-MEM containing 30% L929 cell CM for 6 days.

To generate bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs), bone marrow cells were cultured in BMMC medium, consisting of RPMI 1640 with 2 mM L-glutamine, 10% fetal bovine serum, 1 mM sodium pyruvate, 0.1 mM nonessential amino acids, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 mg/ml streptomycin, 0.05 mmol 2-mercaptoethanol, 25 mM HEPES, 10 ng/ml IL-3 (#213-13, PeproTech, Cranbury, NJ, USA), and 10 ng/ml SCF (#250-03, PeproTech). After 4 weeks of culture, cells were stained to verify the surface expression of anti-FcεRI (#14-5898-82, MAR-1) and anti-CD117 (#17-1171-82, 2B8, both from eBioscience). Cells with >95% purity were used for further experiments.

Cell migration was analyzed using Transwell migration assay chambers (#REF353504, Corning, Steuben, NY, USA). Cells (2 × 10⁵) were seeded into the upper chamber of a 24-well plate fitted with an 8 μm pore polyethylene terephthalate membrane insert (#353097, Corning) in serum-free medium. The lower chamber was filled with different chemoattractants depending on the cell type and experimental condition. For macrophage migration, mast cell–conditioned medium (MC-CM), obtained from mast cells primed with adipocyte-conditioned medium (adipocyte CM), was added to the lower chamber with or without the galectin-3 inhibitor GB1211 (#HY-147041, MedChemExpress, Monmouth Junction, NJ, USA). For mast cell migration, the lower chamber was filled with either LTB 4 or adipocyte CM, with or without the LTB 4 receptor antagonist CP-105696 (#HY-19193, MedChemExpress). Cells were incubated for 6 to 24 h at 37 °C. After incubation, the membranes separating the chambers were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min and stained with crystal violet for another 20 min.

To assess the expression of F4/80, CD11b and CD11c on BMMs and FcεRI and CD117 on mast cells, the cells were incubated in FACS buffer containing 2% FBS and Fc Block (#14-0161-82, eBioscience) for 30 min at 4 °C. They were then stained with fluorescently labeled primary antibodies or control IgG for 30 min at 4 °C. The primary antibodies used included APC-conjugated PDGFRα (#17-1401-81, eBioscience), FITC-conjugated F4/80 (#14-4801-82, eBioscience), APC-conjugated CD11b (#101212, BioLegend), PE-conjugated CD11c (#553802, BD Biosciences), FITC-conjugated anti-FcεRI (#14-5898-82 MAR-1, eBioscience), and APC-conjugated anti-CD117 (#17-1171-82 2B8, eBioscience). After staining, cells were gently washed three times, resuspended in FACS buffer, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. They were then analyzed using an Accuri flow cytometer and a FACSCalibur™ instrument (BD Biosciences). Unstained, single-stained, and fluorescence-minus-one controls were used to set compensation and gating parameters.

Bone marrow-derived mast cells were subjected to electroporation at 300 mV for 30 msec using an Amaxa Nucleofector II (Lonza Bioscience, Waltham, MA, USA). After electroporation, cells were cultured overnight in antibiotic-free growth medium. For the knockdown experiment, siRNAs targeting Sirt6 or galectin-3 (siCtrl, #SN-1003; siSirt6, #50721; siLgals3, #16854; all from Bioneer, Daejeon, Korea) and shRNAs targeting galectins (shLgals3, #3LVS(LVshRNA)-C-16854-21; shLgals9, #3LVS(LVshRNA)-C-16859-21; VectorBuilder, Chicago, IL, USA) were introduced into CD117 + SVFs and HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Invitrogen). The GFP signal in live mast cells was visualized using a Leica DM750 microscope (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany).

Cells were cross-linked by incubating the cells in 1% formaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature. Cross-linking was stopped by incubating the cells with 125 mM glycine for 5 min. The ChIP assay was performed using ChIP Enzymatic Chromatin IP Kit (#9004, Cell Signaling Technology, Beverly, MA, USA). Chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C with antibodies against Sirt6 (#12486, 1:250 dilution), NF-κB (#8242, 1:250 dilution), nonspecific IgG (#2729, 1:250 dilution, all from Cell Signaling Technology), and Ac-H3K9 (#H9286, 1:250 dilution, Sigma-Aldrich). qPCR was performed on ChIP DNA to assess the occupancy of Sirt6 or Ac-H3K9 at the Lgals3 and Lgals9 promoters. Data were normalized to the input.

To obtain total RNA, frozen adipose tissues, BMMs or mast cells were subjected to TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) extraction. The RNA was then precipitated with isopropanol, desiccated using 70% ethanol, and reconstituted in diethyl pyrocarbonate-treated distilled water. First-strand cDNA was synthesized with the random hexamer primer provided in the first-strand cDNA synthesis kit (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). Specific primers were designed using PrimerBank ( https://pga.mgh.harvard.edu/primerbank , Supplementary Table ). qPCR reactions were carried out in a final volume of 10 µl, comprising 10 ng of reverse-transcribed total RNA, 200 nM of both forward and reverse primers, and PCR master mixture. The qPCR analysis was conducted in 384-well plates using the ABI Prism 7900HT Sequence Detection System (Applied Biosystems).

Tissues and cells were homogenized in Tissue Protein Extraction Reagent or Mammalian Protein Extraction Reagent (Thermo, Waltham, MA, USA). Homogenates (20 μg of total protein) were then separated by 10–15% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. Following blocking with 5% skim milk, the blots were probed with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table ). Immunoreactive bands were detected using a Las-4000 imager (GE Healthcare Life Science, Pittsburgh, PA, USA).

All experiments requiring statistical analysis were performed at least three times with similar results. Data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Sample sizes (typically n = 6–8 per group) were determined based on pilot studies and power analyses using G*Power software (α = 0.05, power = 0.8, effect size d = 1.5), and our sample sizes are similar to those reported in previous publications ,, . Data from animal and cell studies were collected in a randomized and blinded fashion, and no data were excluded during the statistical analysis. Data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested.

For comparisons between two groups, Student’s unpaired t test was employed. In the single-cell dataset, comparisons between two groups were determined by the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple comparisons test. Two independent variables were compared using two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s post hoc analysis. The Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated for continuous variables. The statistical significance of gene ontology analysis was calculated by Fisher’s exact test. The exact p -value is indicated on the graph, and a p -value less than 0.05 was considered significant. We utilized GraphPad 9.5 software for statistical analysis.

Further information on research design is available in the linked to this article.

title: Diet-Induced Obesity Increases Monocyte/Macrophage Proliferation during Skin Wound Healing in Mice.
abstract: Obesity is associated with low-grade chronic inflammation and impaired glucose metabolism, both of which are detrimental to wound healing. C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) plays an important role in cell recruitment during healing, and our recent studies revealed the significance of CCR2-CCL2 signaling in promoting the proliferation of pro-inflammatory monocytes/macrophages in wounds. Therefore, we sought to determine whether diet-induced obesity increases monocyte/macrophage proliferation and their accumulation in skin wounds. We first confirmed that wound closure was delayed in obese CCR2RFP/+ mice fed with a high-fat diet (HFD) compared to mice fed with a normal diet (ND). Using in vivo imaging and flow cytometry analysis, we found that HFD mice had significantly increased accumulation of CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages, particularly pro-inflammatory CCR2+Ly6C+ cells in wounds compared to their ND counterparts. Importantly, HFD mice exhibited an increased proliferation of wound CCR2+Ly6C+ compared to ND mice. Together, our data suggest that obesity leads to an increased proliferation and accumulation of pro-inflammatory CCR2+Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds, which may contribute to delayed healing.

sections.results:
Obesity is a major health issue throughout the world, affecting millions of people, increasing the risk of many chronic diseases, and incurring staggering healthcare costs []. Obesity and associated chronic inflammation impair the healing of various tissues and organs, including skin [,]. Accumulating evidence indicates that obesity can disrupt all stages of skin wound healing, including inflammation, proliferation and remodeling phases, both in humans and in animal models [,,,].

Cells from the monocyte/macrophage lineage are recognized as prominent players that orchestrate many biological processes important for wound healing, including pathogen killing, phagocytosis of debris and dead cells, promoting inflammation and its resolution, the proliferation and migration of other wound cells, and wound remodeling, all helping to restore homeostasis to the wound environment during efficient wound healing [,,]. However, the persistent accumulation of pro-inflammatory monocytes/macrophages in diabetic wounds leads to chronic inflammation and impaired healing [,].

C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2), is a receptor for several C-C motif monocyte chemokines, including CCL2, CCL7, and CCL8 []. Upon the appearance of an injury, CCR2+ monocytes quickly infiltrate the wound bed from peripheral blood, at least in part due to the aforementioned chemokines [,]. Previous studies have demonstrated the importance of CCR2 in normal skin wound healing; CCR2-deficient mice exhibit significantly delayed healing []. However, CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages have also been reported to promote inflammation and obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction in various tissues [,,,]. Although macrophage accumulation is generally thought to be due to monocyte infiltration from peripheral blood, primarily as a result of the CCL2-CCR2 axis, we recently showed that CCL2-CCR2 signaling also induces proliferation of Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds [,]. However, whether obesity impacts such proliferation remains to be determined.

Therefore, we designed current study to determine whether proliferation contributes to the accumulation of CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds, using the diet-induced obese mouse model. Using in vivo imaging and flow cytometry analysis, our data indicated that obese mice had significantly delayed healing compared to lean controls, which was associated with increased accumulation of CCR2+ cells in wounds, particularly pro-inflammatory Ly6C+CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages. Importantly, obesity increased proliferation of these pro-inflammatory Ly6C+F4/80lo/-CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages, which may contribute to the delayed healing in obese mice.

Homozygous B6.129(Cg)-Ccr2 tm2.1Ifc /J mice and C57Bl/6 were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA) and crossbred to generate heterozygous B6.129(Cg)-Ccr2 tm2.1Ifc /J (CCR2 RFP/+ ) mice in which CCR2+ cells express red fluorescent protein (RFP) to allow tracking of these cells. For the induction of diet-induced obesity, male and female CCR2 RFP/+ mice (n = 15–17/group/sex) were fed a high-fat diet (HFD, 60 Kcal% fat, 7% Kcal/fructose, Research Diets) ad libitum for 12 weeks, beginning at 8 weeks of age; mice were thus ~20 weeks old at the time of wounding. Age-matched lean CCR2 RFP/+ mice received a standard chow diet (ND; n = 15–17/group/sex). All mice were housed in environmentally controlled conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle. Water and food were available ad libitum. All animal studies were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Illinois at Chicago.

At the end of the 12-week feeding period, to confirm the establishment of obesity and glucose intolerance, both HFD and ND mice (n = 8–9/group/sex) were weighed and fasted for 4 h before receiving an i.p. injection of 1 g/kg body weight dextrose. Blood glucose levels were measured from a tail nick immediately before the injection of glucose and at 15, 30, 60, and 90 min thereafter.

HFD and ND mice were subjected to excisional wounding of the dorsal skin with an 8 mm biopsy punch as previously described []. Two wounds were created on the dorsal skin of mice for flow cytometry analysis, while one wound model was used for the evaluation of CCR2+ cell accumulation. Tegaderm (3M, 1626W, St. Paul, MN, USA) was used to cover the wounds until tissue harvest. Wound closure was evaluated by digital pictures using Fiji Image J (v1.49).

The accumulation of CCR2-RFP+ cells in skin wounds was measured using the Xenogen IVIS Spectrum (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA). Following wounding, mice were placed in a light-tight imaging chamber under anesthesia; fluorescence signals of CCR2-RFP were collected at as early as 2 h and up to 14 days post-wounding. The radiation efficiency of fluorescent signals was measured within the wound area throughout the healing process.

Skin wounds, femoral bone marrow cells, and peripheral blood cells were collected on day 3 and 6 post-wounding for flow cytometry analysis. Skin wounds were collected using a 12 mm biopsy punch and immediately dissociated into single-cell suspension by enzymatic digestion as previously described []. Cells were first incubated with Zombie Violet (Biolegend, San Diego, CA, USA) to assess cell viability. Cells from bone marrow and blood were not stained with Zombie dyes due to the low percentage of dead cells (<3%). After Fc receptor blocking with anti-CD16/32 antibody (Biolegend, clone S17011E), skin cells were labeled with anti-Ly6G−BV605 (Biolegend, clone 1A8), CD11b−APC/Fire750 (Biolegend, clone CBRM1/5), F4/80−FITC (Biolegend, clone BM8), and Ly6C−Percp/cy5.5 (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA, clone AL−21) antibodies; cells from bone marrow and blood were stained with anti-Ly6G−BV421, CD11b−APC/Fire750, CD115−APC (Biolegend, clone AFS98), and Ly6C−Percp/cy5.5 antibodies.

For proliferation analysis, mice were administrated with 2 mg BrdU (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA, B9285) via i.v. injection through the retro-orbital vein on day 3 and day 6 post-wounding. At 4 h post-BrdU injection, mice were sacrificed for cell proliferation analysis in skin wounds, bone marrow, and peripheral blood. After surface staining of markers, cells were fixed, permeabilized, incubated with DNase-I (Sigma) using a BD Cytofix/Cytoperm™ kit, then incubated with anti-BrdU-FITC antibody (Biolegend). For cells from skin wounds, cells were incubated with FxCycle TM Far Red (ThermoFisher Scientific, Grand Island, NY, USA) 30 min before acquisition, following the manufacturer’s instructions. All samples were analyzed on LSR Fortessa with HTS (BD Biosciences) cytometer. Data were analyzed using FlowJo (FlowJo LLC, Ashland, OR, USA).

Data are expressed as mean ± SEM. Statistical significance of differences was evaluated by Mann–Whitney test or ANOVA. A value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

To investigate the effects of obesity on wound healing, we fed both male and female CCR2 RFP/+ mice with HFD for 12 weeks. As expected, both male and female HFD mice developed obesity, as indicated by a significantly higher body weight than the ND controls (male—HFD 50.1 g ± 1.5 g vs. ND 31.5 g ± 0.7 g, p < 0.0001; female—HFD 44.9 g ± 1.5 g vs. ND 24.6 ± 0.5 g, p < 0.0001). Additionally, all HFD mice showed impaired tolerance to glucose challenge compared to the ND controls (A,B). Next, we created two full-thickness excisional wounds on the dorsal skin of the HFD and ND mice. As shown in C–E, HFD mice showed a significantly delayed wound closure compared to the ND controls in both male and female mice, particularly at the later stage of healing. No significant differences were observed between male and female mice in glucose tolerance () or wound closure () in either HFD or ND mice. Together, our data confirmed glucose intolerance and impaired healing in both male and female mice fed a long-term HFD.

Previous studies have indicated that CCR2 plays an important role in monocyte/macrophage recruitment and promotes inflammation during skin wound healing []. Therefore, we assessed the effects of obesity on the accumulation of CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages throughout the healing process. To assess CCR2+ cell accumulation in wounds, we utilized CCR2 RFP/+ mice for which fluorescent cells within the injured area can be tracked by in vivo imaging (A,C). In response to injury, CCR2+ cells infiltrated into the wound as early as day 1 post-wounding (B,D). Interestingly, the accumulation of wound CCR2+ cells appeared to be delayed in male HFD mice, as the RFP signal was lower in HFD wounds than the ND counterparts on day 1 post-wounding; however, this delay was not observed in female mice (B,D). During later stages of healing, the CCR2+ cell signal dissipated in the wounds of ND mice, but both male and female HFD mice showed a persistent accumulation of CCR2+ cells, with significantly higher RFP signals detected in wounds on day 5, 7, and 9 post-wounding compared with the ND controls (B,D). Interestingly, the accumulation of CCR2+ cells in wounds was significantly higher in HFD male mice compared to HFD female mice at the early stages of healing, but this difference did not persist as healing progressed and was not evident in ND mice ().

We also performed flow cytometry analysis of skin wound cells isolated from male CCR2 RFP/+ mice fed either ND or HFD to corroborate the fluorescent imaging data. On day 6 post-wounding, there was a trend towards a higher percentage of CCR2+ cells in HFD mice compared to the ND controls ( p = 0.08, E,F); although this difference did not reach statistical significance, the trend was consistent with our observation by IVIS imaging. Together, our data demonstrated that HFD induced a persistent elevation of CCR2+ cells associated with the impaired healing of skin wounds.

Since CCR2 can be expressed on cells other than monocytes/macrophages, we conducted flow cytometry analysis to investigate CCR2 expression specifically on two well-defined macrophage/monocyte populations that play important roles both in normal and impaired wound healing [,]. In response to injury, both the pro-inflammatory CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages (Live Ly6G-CD11b+F4/80lo/-Ly6C+CCR2+) and mature macrophages (Live Ly6G-CD11b+F4/80+Ly6C-CCR2+) quickly accumulated in skin wounds (B). Consistent with genetically obese mice [], male HFD mice exhibited a significantly higher accumulation of pro-inflammatory CCR2+Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds compared to ND controls on day 3 post-wounding, while mature CCR2+F4/80+Ly6C- macrophages did not show significant differences between HFD and ND mice (C).

Since CCR2+ monocytes are generated in bone marrow and travel through peripheral blood to reach the wound site [], we also evaluated changes in CCR2+ monocytes after wounding in these tissues in HFD and ND mice. As shown in D, the numbers of circulating CCR2+ monocytes (Ly6G-CD11b+CD115+Ly6C+CCR2+) were significantly higher in HFD mice than their ND counterparts on day 3 post-wounding. In contrast, the numbers of bone marrow CCR2+ monocytes (Ly6G-CD11b+CD115+Ly6C+CCR2+) were comparable between HFD and ND mice regardless of time points of wounding (E). Moreover, the intermediate monocyte population (Ly6G-CD11b+CD115+Ly6C-CCR2+) was significantly elevated in the bone marrow of the HFD mice compared with ND controls on day 6 post-wounding (E). In summary, these data indicated that HFD leads to the increased accumulation of pro-inflammatory CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages in wounds, which is associated with elevated circulating CCR2+Ly6C+ monocytes in blood.

In addition to the infiltration of blood monocytes, our previous studies demonstrated an important contribution of monocyte/macrophage proliferation to their accumulation in the skin wounds of non-obese mice, which is enhanced in genetically obese and diabetic mice [,]. Thus, we sought to determine whether monocyte/macrophage proliferation was also increased in the wounds of HFD mice. Unfortunately, the CCR2-RFP signal was lost after the cell fixation and permeabilization process needed for assessing proliferation. Therefore, we were unable to use this marker in our proliferation assay. All mice were administered BrdU, and cell proliferation was evaluated by flow cytometry analysis of BrdU and cell cycle dye labeling at 4 h post-injection (A). Consistent with our previous findings in genetically obese mice, HFD mice showed significantly higher numbers of pro-inflammatory monocytes/macrophages at the S/G2/M phases of the cell cycle on day 3 post-wounding compared to the ND controls, with a similar trend towards higher proliferation on day 6 ( p = 0.06). In contrast, mature macrophages maintained a low proliferation rate in the skin wounds of both HFD and ND mice (B). In blood and bone marrow, the numbers of cells incorporating BrdU were not significantly different between HFD and ND mice at any day post-wounding (C,D). In short, our data indicate that HFD increases the proliferation of pro-inflammatory CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds but not in peripheral blood nor in bone marrow.

Obesity leads to persistent accumulation of monocytes/macrophages and chronic inflammation in skin wounds, contributing to impaired healing [,]. In this study, we utilized in vivo imaging and flow cytometry analysis to track the accumulation and proliferation of CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds. Our data demonstrated increased proliferation of pro-inflammatory Ly6C+CCR2+ monocytes/macrophages in wounds of HFD mice compared to ND controls, contributing to their persistent accumulation as well as delayed healing.

Obesity leads to chronic low-grade inflammation and dysregulated glucose metabolism, both of which are detrimental to wound healing in humans and rodents [,,]. Our group and others have previously demonstrated sustained inflammation, including persistent accumulation of inflammatory monocytes/macrophages and impaired healing of skin wounds in genetically obese and diabetic db/db mice [,,]. Mice fed a HFD, which is considered a model of obesity and insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, have also been reported to be associated with delayed healing [,]. In our study, we confirmed delayed healing in HFD mice associated with glucose intolerance. Using in vivo imaging andCCR2 RFP/+ mice, we demonstrated increased accumulation CCR2+ cells in wounds of HFD mice compared to ND mice during the mid-proliferative to late stages of healing. Moreover, flow cytometry analysis confirmed the in vivo imaging data, demonstrating that obesity increased accumulation of pro-inflammatory CCR2+monocytes/macrophages (CCR2+Ly6C+) but not mature macrophages (CCR2+Ly6C-F4/80+) in wounds. These data indicate that obesity may influence healing via a persistent inflammatory response, resulting from sustained accumulation of pro-inflammatory monocytes/macrophages.

CCR2 plays important roles in cell chemotaxis and promoting the inflammatory response during wound healing in mice []. Along with increased Ly6C+CCR2+ cells in skin wounds, we also observed elevated levels of circulating CCR2+CD115+Ly6C+ in the peripheral blood of HFD mice compared with ND controls on day 3 post-injury, suggesting that obesity increases production and/or mobilization of these cells in bone marrow. Indeed, previous studies have shown that obesity can modify the production and epigenetics of myeloid progenitor cells in bone marrow and in turn leads to leukocytosis and inflammation in peripheral tissues [,]. In addition, our recent studies demonstrated that wound Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages proliferate locally, which contributes to their accumulation in wounds [], while diabetes leads to significantly elevated proliferation of Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages, contributing to their persistent accumulation in these mice []. Importantly, this process is likely driven by the CCL2-CCR2 signaling pathway that is enhanced in diabetic mice []. Interestingly, in the diet-induced obese model, we also observed significantly more CCR2+Ly6C+ cells at S/G2/M stages of the cell cycle in wounds in HFD than ND mice on day 3 post-injury, while this number was comparable on day 6, suggesting that the increased accumulation of CCR2+Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages may result from increased proliferation in wounds as well as increased infiltration from blood.

Although it is possible that monocytes could incorporate BrdU in bone marrow and quickly emigrate to the wound bed, we did not detect significant differences in BrdU+ monocytes between HFD vs. ND mice in either bone marrow or peripheral blood, suggesting that Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages proliferate in wounds. Moreover, differences in the impact of HFD on monocyte proliferation between bone marrow, blood, and wounds indicated that the wound environment, instead of cell-intrinsic factors, is key for inducing monocyte/macrophage proliferation in skin wounds. Indeed, previous studies have highlighted environmental factors which may affect macrophage proliferation in tissues, including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-4, and M-CSF [,,,]. Nonetheless, obesity likely impacts many different cells and pathways, and we cannot exclude contributions to monocyte/macrophage accumulation in wounds and impaired healing by other factors in HFD versus ND mice, and the mechanisms involved requires further study. Such mechanisms could involve altered monopoiesis in bone marrow or altered trafficking to wounds, as well as proliferation in wounds [,,,]. Finally, we note that the time point of peak proliferation differed between diet-induced obese versus genetic diabetes models, which could be due to the difference in severity of diabetes and chronic inflammation in these models [,]. Whether CCL2-CCR2 signaling promotes monocyte/macrophage proliferation in wounds of HFD mice as it does in diabetic db/db mice remains to be determined.

We note that previous studies reported that initial expansion of the adipose tissue macrophage pool in early-stage HFD-induced obesity in mice was due primarily to the proliferation of resident cells [,]. During the progression of obesity with continued HFD, both infiltration and proliferation contributed to further adipose tissue macrophage expansion. We also observed an early increase in the proliferation of wound monocytes/macrophages in HFD mice, consistent with the adipose tissue studies. Whether there is crosstalk between subcutaneous adipose tissue macrophages and wound macrophages is an intriguing question and awaits further study [,,].

Finally, sex differences have been reported in previous studies of obesity-associated complications, as female mice were protected from HFD-induced metabolic dysfunction [,]. However, the influence of sex on skin wound healing remains unclear [,,]. In the present study, diet-matched male and female CCR2 RFP/+ mice showed no differences in glucose tolerance or wound closure. CCR2+ cell accumulation was increased in wounds of HFD male mice compared to HFD female mice at early stages of healing; however, no significant differences were observed between sexes at later stages of healing. In the end, the altered early CCR2+ cell accumulation between sexes did not appear to influence the kinetics of wound closure.

In summary, our study demonstrated that diet-induced obesity and pre-diabetes leads to the increased proliferation of pro-inflammatory CCR2+Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages in skin wounds, contributing to their enhanced accumulation of in these wounds. Future studies should explore the underlying mechanisms of this obesity-associated increase in monocyte/macrophage behaviors and the inhibition of such changes to improve healing.

title: c-Abl inhibition mitigates diet-induced obesity through improving insulin sensitivity of subcutaneous fat in mice.
abstract: AIMS/HYPOTHESIS: High-energy diets are among the main causes of the global epidemic of metabolic disorders, including obesity and type 2 diabetes. The mechanisms of high-energy-diet-induced metabolic disorders are complex and largely unknown. The non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-Abl plays an important role in adipogenesis in vitro but its role in vivo in the regulation of metabolism is still elusive. Hence, we sought to address the role of c-Abl in diet-induced obesity and obesity-associated insulin resistance. METHODS: The expression of c-Abl in different fat tissues from obese humans or mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) were first analysed by western blotting and quantitative PCR. We employed conditional deletion of the c-Abl gene (also known as Abl1) in adipose tissue using Fabp4-Cre and 6-week-old mice were fed with either a chow diet (CD) or an HFD. Age-matched wild-type mice were treated with the c-Abl inhibitor nilotinib or with vehicle and exposed to either CD or HFD, followed by analysis of body mass, fat mass, glucose and insulin tolerance. Histological staining, ELISA and biochemical analysis were used to clarify details of changes in physiology and molecular signalling. RESULTS: c-Abl was highly expressed in subcutaneous fat from obese humans and HFD-induced obese mice. Conditional knockout of c-Abl in adipose tissue improved insulin sensitivity and mitigated HFD-induced body mass gain, hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia. Consistently, treatment with nilotinib significantly reduced fat mass and improved insulin sensitivity in HFD-fed mice. Further biochemical analyses suggested that c-Abl inhibition improved whole-body insulin sensitivity by reducing HFD-triggered insulin resistance and increasing adiponectin in subcutaneous fat. CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION: Our findings define a new biological role for c-Abl in the regulation of diet-induced obesity through improving insulin sensitivity of subcutaneous fat. This suggests it may become a novel therapeutic target in the treatment of metabolic disorders.
