sections.other:
The dramatic increase in the world-wide prevalence of obesity is recognized as a risk factor for development of numerous complicated co-morbidities . Research has uncovered an important role for adipose tissue not only as an energy-storage organ but also as a potent source of inflammatory mediators including leptin, TNF-α and macrophage-attractant chemokines (MCP1, MIP-1 and MIF) . During obesity, the release of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines from adipose tissue may re-program resident immune cells towards an augmented inflammatory profile and may result in the recruitment of immune cell populations that are otherwise under-represented . Consequently, the development of chronic, low-grade inflammation associated with obesity may exacerbate inflammatory diseases in other tissues and organs .

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease characterized by the progressive destruction of bile ducts that can lead to portal hypertension . The pathogenesis of PSC remains unknown however an autoimmune origin is widely accepted . A close relationship exists with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) as PSC is considered one of the extraintestinal manifestations of IBD . Up to 80% of patients with PSC also have IBD whereas approximately 7% of IBD patients may develop PSC , . Unfortunately, no effective treatment strategies exist and the persistent liver inflammation associated with PSC can lead to fibrosis requiring liver transplantation or the development of cholangiocarcinoma (CC) . Continued examination of genetic and environmental factors such as diet and lifestyle triggering chronic, uncontrolled inflammation is required to understand the pathogenesis of PSC and for the development of effective therapeutics.

We have previously identified a subpopulation of patients based on body mass index (BMI) who are overweight (BMI 25–30) or obese (BMI >30) with PSC that had more advanced fibrosis at presentation and more rapid fibrosis progression as measured by ultrasound transient elastography (Fig. ) . However, the link between obesity and more severe PSC has yet to be examined. In this current study we explored the impact of diet-induced obesity during the development of cholangitis by using an antigen-specific murine model of PSC. In addition we identified IL-15 in our model as a critical factor driving inflammation and tissue damage within the livers of obese mice with cholangitis. IL-15 has been linked to the promotion of lipolysis and energy expenditure while at the same time is responsible for the maintenance and survival of T cells and NK cells , . To date, the role of IL-15 in PSC and biliary diseases has been poorly examined. Therefore we evaluated the neutralization of IL-15 in our murine model to gain greater insight into the underlying pathways triggering or accelerating PSC in individuals with obesity in order to identify potential novel therapeutic targets.

sections.methods:
The study protocol was approved by the University of Calgary Animal Care Committee and conformed to the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals . Mouse studies were carried out using a modified protocol of the OVAbil model previously described . Briefly, C57BL/6 mice that express ovalbumin peptide (aminoacids 139–385) in a cholangiocyte-restricted manner (OVAbil) were obtained from Dr. Marion G. Peters and used as recipient mice. To induce biliary inflammation, MHC I- and MHC II-restricted OVA-specific T cells (OT) were transferred from the lymphocyte fraction recovered by Percoll gradient from the spleens of donor mice. Recipient OVAbil mice were given 10 7 cells from each OT I and OT II donor mice via intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection. Five or 10 days after transfer, mice were sacrificed under deep anesthesia and degree of disease was assessed.

Seven to eight week-old male and female OVAbil mice were fed standard chow (SC; 3.8 kcal/g) or a custom high-fat/high-sucrose diet (HFD; 4.6 kcal/g) for twelve weeks (Dyets Inc, USA) . Weight gain was recorded weekly and circulating leptin was measured as a putative marker of increasing adiposity in HFD fed mice.

At indicated time points (before T cells transfer and 5 or 10 days post transfer) mice were anesthetized (Isoflurane) and whole blood was collected via cardiac puncture. Blood samples were centrifuged and serum was stored at −80 °C for future analysis. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels were measured by Calgary Laboratory Services (Calgary, AB, Canada). Quantification of cytokines and chemokines was conducted as reported using a commercial mouse cytokine 31-plex Discovery Assay (Eve Technologies, Calgary, AB, Canada) . The analytes included: eotaxin, G-CSF, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-7, IL-9, IL-10, IL-12(p40), IL-12(p70), IL-13, IL-15, IL-17, IP-10, KC, LIF, MCP-1, MIG, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, MIP-2, RANTES, TNF-α and VEGF. Briefly, 31 analytes were simultaneously tested in a single well using multiplexing LASER Bead Technology and colour-coded polystyrene beads. Using dual-laser technology and flow cytometry the analyte can be identified based on the bead colour whereas the concentration of analyte present is quantified by the fluorescent intensity using a standard curve. Values are presented in pg/ml.

At sacrifice liver tissue was excised and rapidly fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for histological assessment. To assess bile duct (BD) inflammation and damage, five portal tracts were randomly scored as follows: inflammation (0–3) 0, no visible inflammatory cells; 1 low number of inflammatory cells; 2 mild inflammation; 3 severe inflammation. BD damage (0–2) 0 BD architecture preserved; 1 loss of typical BD architecture (deranged with infiltrating cells displacing cholangiocytes); 2 absent BD.

Fresh liver tissue was placed in cold, sterile PBS with 10% FBS and 2 mM EDTA and immediately homogenized using a gentleMACS tissue dissociator (Miltenyi Biotec Inc, Germany). Tissue homogenate was filtered through a 60 micron mesh to achieve a single cell suspension. Following centrifugation, cells were layered on a 33%/77% Percoll gradient and spun at room temperature at 600 rcf for 20 minutes (GE Healthcare Bio-Sciences AB, Uppsala Sweden). Leukocytes were removed from the gradient, pelleted and resuspended in cold FACS buffer (PBS, 0.5% BSA and 2 mM EDTA) followed by incubation with the following fluorescent-conjugated antibodies: Panel 1; APC/Cy7-Ly6C, PO-CD11b, PE/Cy7-F4/80, PE-Ly6G, FITC-CX3CR1, PerCP-CCR5, APC-CCR1. Panel 2; APC-CD3. PB- CD4, PO-CD8, PE-NK1.1. Data were acquired on a FACS Aria II (BD Biosciences) and analyzed with Kaluza software (Beckman Coulter, USA).

Transcripts of canonical markers of fibrosis were assayed in liver tissue. Briefly, small pieces (~20 mg) of liver tissue were homogenized in TRizol® reagent (Invitrogen, USA) and total RNA was extracted by the chloroform method. The concentration of total RNA was quantified by NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc, Mississauga, ON, Canada) followed by reverse transcription using the RT2 first strand cDNA synthesis kit for RT-PCR (Qiagen, Toronto, ON, Canada). The resultant cDNA was amplified using primers generated through the Universal ProbeLibrary (Roche Diagnostics, Laval, QC, Canada) and synthesized by the University of Calgary Core DNA Services (Calgary, AB, Canada). A StepOne Real-Time PCR System was used for the real-time PCR reactions (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc, Mississauga, ON, Canada) and FAM detection probes (Roche Diagnostics, Laval, QC, Canada). The following primer sequences were used: α-smooth muscle actin ( sma ) 5′-CTCTCTTCCAGCCATCTTTCAT-3′, 5′-CGTAGGTGCTTTGGTGGATAT-3′; tissue inhibitor of matrix metalloproteases -1 ( timp1 ) 5′-GCAAAGAGCTTTCTCAAAGACC-3′, 5′- TCACAAAGGGACAAATAGATAGGGA-3′; type 1 collagen ( col1a1 ) 5′ CATGTTCAGCTTTGTGGACCT-3′ 5′- TGTAGGGACTTCAGTCGACG-3′; β-actin (housekeeping) 5′-CTAAGGCCAACCGTGAAA-3′, 5′-AGGGACATACGGAGACCA-3′.

In order to neutralize IL-15 bioactivity, mice were treated with anti-IL-15 antibodies (clone GRW15PLZ, eBioscience USA) as previously reported . Briefly, 5 µg of anti-IL-15 or isotype-matched antibodies were injected i.p. daily from day 4 to day 9 post- OVA-specific T cell transfer and disease outcome was assessed on day 10 in experimental groups.

Data are shown as mean ± SE. Differences between mouse groups was determined by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s posthoc for multiple comparisons or when indicated student’s t test. p < 0.05 was accepted as significantly different.

All data generated or analyzed during this study are included in this published article (and its Supplementary Information files).
sections.results:
Experimental groups fed either SC or HFD showed clear changes in bodyweight and leptin secretion over time. Given the male-dominant phenomenon in patients with PSC we started our project by studying female and male mice separately. In terms of bodyweight, we did not see significant differences between sexes after the 12 week-diet administration. Female mice fed SC gained 27.3% (+5.8 g) of the initial weight and female mice fed a HFD gained 49.3% (+11.5 g) of initial weight, whereas male mice fed SC gained 20% of initial weight (+5.3 g) and male mice fed HFD gained 46.6% (+13.8 g). Thus, other than natural sex-specific bodyweight differences we observed similar weight gain in both male and female mice (Fig. ).

As leptin is secreted in proportion to body fat by adipocytes we used leptin levels as an indirect measurement of changes in adiposity in the mice. We observed a dramatic difference in serum leptin levels between SC and HFD fed animals over the 12-week period (Fig. ). Interestingly, when comparing leptin levels between female and male within the HFD group, we found significant differences on week 6 post-diet (i.e. males had higher levels of leptin than female counterparts), however under the long-term feeding regime leptin concentrations in female mice reached comparable levels to male mice on week 12 (Fig. ). The fact that female mice exhibited similar levels of leptin upon long-term HFD feeding compared to male mice suggests that this may be true for additional inflammatory cytokines and may account in part for losing sex differences in our mouse studies. Thus, mouse results are presented as SC group versus HFD group given no differences between male and female groups were observed.

Diet-induced obese OVAbil mice were employed to assess the relationship between obesity and experimental PSC. Following obesity induction, HFD fed OVAbil mice developed macromolecular steatosis as evident by the accumulation of large lipid droplets within hepatocytes while the bile ducts (BDs) exhibited preserved architecture prior to OVA-T cell transfer (Fig. ). Liver sections from mice fed SC revealed uniform liver parenchyma with well-defined bile BDs before the transfer of OVA-T cells (Fig. ). Five days following adoptive transfer, increased periportal infiltrating cells were seen in HFD fed OVAbil mice compared to chow fed mice that displayed few infiltrating inflammatory cells in the portal tracts and preserved BDs (Fig. ). At the peak of disease (day 10 post-transfer), the majority of the portal tracts in HFD OVAbil mice were reduced and most of the BDs were absent whereas mice fed SC showed increased size in periportal inflammatory foci resulting in reduced portal tract space but still visible BDs (Fig. ). The degree of inflammation (p = 0.001) and BD damage was significantly increased in HFD fed mice compared to SC fed mice after 10 days post transfer (p = 0.0002, Fig. ). Using ALT serum levels as a putative liver damage indicator, we observed a trend for elevated ALT levels at the peak of the disease as compared to baseline levels (before transfer of OVA-specific T cells) while there were no significant differences between SC and HFD mice (Fig. ). However, unlike SC mice, significant weight loss was observed in the obese mice (−0.3% vs −8.1% of initial weight in average, respectively) (Fig. ).

To the best of our knowledge this is the first time experimental PSC has been examined in the context of obesity. In order to further understand the exacerbated disease phenotype in obese OVAbil mice we characterized infiltrating immune cells in the liver using flow cytometry. The specific gating strategy is shown in supplemental data (Fig. ). Macrophages are one of the most studied immune cell populations in liver. Others and we have reported gene-profiling data of inflammatory and restorative macrophage subpopulations during liver injury processes underscoring important differences between these cell types , . We aimed to determine changes in this population in the context of obesity before and after induction of immune-mediated cholangitis. Macrophage populations were broadly subdivided based on Ly6C antigen expression. Upon gating CD11b + myeloid cells, an apparent segregation of F4/80+ Ly6C hi and Ly6C lo macrophage subpopulations was observed (Fig. ). Others have reported this same strategy to classify newly recruited (Ly6C hi ) versus long-term resident (Ly6C lo ) populations . The majority (>80%) of the Ly6C + populations were CCR2 + with a few CX3CR1 + (Fig. ). Mice fed SC initially presented an abundant Ly6C lo macrophage population (85% of myeloid CD11b + cells), which upon liver injury induction (i.e. 5 days post- OVA-specific T cells transfer) showed a dramatic reduction (∼50%) however, five days later a clear recovery of this population occurred in mice fed SC (Figs ,). Mice fed HFD displayed reduced numbers of Ly6C lo macrophages but in sharp contrast these animals did not display the capacity to re-populate the liver with Ly6C lo macrophages (Fig. ). In terms of Ly6C hi macrophages, one of the expected sources of restorative Ly6C lo macrophages, HFD animals showed lower but not significant numbers as compared to SC-fed mice on day 10 post- T cell transfer as well (23 ± 3 vs 31 ± 2.5, p = 0.07) (Fig. ).

Prior to OVA-T cells transfer, we identified few neutrophils present in the liver of SC fed mice whereas animals fed HFD exhibited higher numbers of neutrophils than SC mice (0.7 ± 0.1vs 0.1 ± 0.07, respectively) (Figs , ). As cholangitis progressed, increasing numbers of neutrophils were observed in both groups however greater infiltration of neutrophils was consistently seen in obese OVAbil mice reaching the maximum on day 10 post-transfer (HFD 18 ± 5.6 vs SC 5.1 ± 2) (Figs , ). In addition to the heightened infiltration of neutrophils in the liver of obese mice, these cells exhibited a different phenotype lacking surface expression of CCR1 and CCR5 compared to neutrophils recovered from SC-fed OVAbil mice. Neutrophils from SC mice (∼50%) were CCR1 + CCR5 + double positive whereas most of the neutrophils from HFD animals (70%) lacked both chemokine receptors (Fig. ).

To initiate and amplify inflammatory diseases, infiltration of cells with cytotoxic potential such as CD8 + T cells is often required. Thus, we aimed to determine the extent of infiltration during experimental PSC in obese mice. Prior to biliary damage, there were low numbers of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells within the liver with a clear CD4 + T cell predominance (Fig. ). Five days after OVA-specific T cell transfer, a clear expansion of both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells was found (Fig. ). By day 10, the number of CD8 + T cells had tripled compared to CD4 + T cells in the HFD group whereas the number of CD8 + T cells was only slightly higher than the CD4 + T cells from the SC group (Fig. ).

Prior to the induction of biliary damage, we observed a significant depletion of CD4 + NKT but not CD4 − CD8 − (double negative) NKT cells resulting from the obesogenic diet. Phenotyping of liver cells in mice fed SC showed ∼21% of lymphocytes were CD4 + NKT cells, in contrast, same analysis showed that obese mice had ∼10% of CD4 + NKT cell population. (Fig. ). Moreover, induction of portal inflammation by transferring OVA-specific T cells led to the progressive loss of CD4 + NKT cells over the time with an exaggerated phenotype in obese mice leading to a virtual depletion at the peak of disease compared to SC fed mice (Fig. ).

Inflammatory cytokines and chemokines have been shown to contribute to liver pathology whereas pharmacological blockade of IL-17 or transgenic mice deficient in IL-12 result in the reduction of liver damage and fibrosis , . To gain insight into changes in cytokines and chemokines resulting from diet-induced obesity in mice with experimental PSC, blood samples were collected and assayed to measure multiple analytes simultaneously. We detected increased production of IL-9, IL-13, IL-15, IL-17 and the granulopoietic factor G-CSF in mice fed the HFD on day 10 compared with mice fed SC (Fig. ). Enhanced levels of TNFα were detected in mice with PSC however no significant difference between diet groups was found. We observed that obese mice had supressed production of IL-1α prior to biliary damage induction and trended towards statistical significance on day 5 compared to SC fed mice (Fig. ). On day 10, both groups showed decreased secretion of IL-1α with a more pronounced effect in obese animals (Fig. ). While biliary damage triggered the release of CCL2, CCL3 and CCL5 on day 10 post-transfer, mice fed HFD showed exaggerated secretion of these chemokines as well as CXCL-10 (Fig. ).

A central role for CD8 + T cells driving experimental PSC in the OVAbil mouse model has been described . In line with this observation, we identified increased numbers of CD8 + T cells at the peak of cholangitis that correlated with elevated circulating levels of IL-15 in obese OVAbil mice. To determine the consequence of increased IL-15, we administered an IL-15 blocking antibody to HFD mice starting on day 4 post-T cell transfers based on our previous observation that CD8+ T cells begin to expand around day 5 post adoptive transfer (Fig. ). Similar to our previous observation, obese OVAbil mice lost significantly more weight than SC mice after adoptive T cell transfer however IL-15 neutralization tended to prevent the majority of weight loss in obese animals only reaching statistical difference on day 10 (Fig. ). In regards of histological damage, HFD mice receiving OVA-specific T cells and isotype control antibody showed periportal and parenchymal inflammatory infiltrate and this was significantly improved to only periportal infiltration with visibly reduced size when we used neutralizing IL-15 antibody treatment (Fig. ). Moreover, blockade of IL-15 modified the plasma cytokine profile compared to obese animals treated with the isotype control. Cytokine profiling revealed important findings, for example IL-1α levels, which were low upon liver damage, notably increased when mice were treated with anti-IL-15 antibody (Fig. ). Also, except for IL-9, cytokines including IL-13, IL-17 and G-CSF were supressed by anti-IL-15 treatment (Fig. ). Inflammatory chemokines were also impacted by neutralization of IL-15, this latter resulted in inhibition of CCL2, CCL3 and CXCL10 secretion.

Flow cytometry analysis revealed that blocking IL-15 in obese mice led to the recovery of previously diminished tolerogenic leukocyte populations such as NKT lymphocytes and macrophages (Fig. ). Ly6C lo macrophages (likely restorative) were prominent whereas the Ly6C hi macrophage population was almost negligible suggesting that IL-15 could be dampening Ly6C hi to Ly6C lo macrophage transition. Also, blockade of IL-15 concomitantly restrained expansion of pathogenic cells like neutrophils and cytotoxic lymphocytes (Fig. ).
sections.discussion:
One of the most concerning outcomes of the obesity pandemic is the increased incidence of co-morbidities including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and liver disease . Recent research has revealed that obesity is associated with more severe development of gastrointestinal disease . The impact of obesity on certain liver pathologies including the development of PSC has not been explored to date.

Our clinical observation identified a group of PSC patients with a strong association between higher BMI and more advanced fibrosis stage suggesting that immune changes accompanying adipocyte hyperplasia and hypertrophy might be accelerating the transition from inflammatory to fibrotic stages of liver disease . To investigate the link between obesity and more severe PSC we examined the development of experimental PSC in obese mice. We confirmed that mice fed HFD had aggravated portal tract damage along with exacerbated biliary damage as gauged by periportal inflammation, portal space reduction and absence (assessed in the majority of portal tracts) of BDs compared to standard chow fed mice.

Expansion of CD8 + T cells has been associated with increased disease severity in this model of immune-mediated cholangitis . As expected we observed expansion of CD8 + T cells upon transfer of pathogenic T cells in non-obese mice. However, mice fed the HFD had an uncontrolled expansion of the same population that correlated with higher levels of IL-15 in the serum. Interleukin-15 is produced by cells from both hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic origin and has been linked to obesity and liver disease . On one hand, IL-15 can exert anti-adipogenic functions and may promote energy expenditure – . However, IL-15 may also lead to the accumulation of lipid within hepatocytes and contribute to the development of non-alcohol fatty liver disease (NAFLD) . Therapeutic blockade of IL-15 in obese mice with cholangitis resulted in attenuated histological damage, lower numbers of infiltrating neutrophils and CD8 + T cells and reduced levels of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines including IL-13, IL-17, C-GSF, CCL2, CCL3 and CXCL10. In PSC, IL-15 may represent the inflammatory switch driving exaggerated biliary damage. While IL-15 levels never disappeared after blockade this is most likely due to constant release in response to rapid clearance and short-term lifespan of the cytokine . Continued examination of the role of IL-15 along with other pathological cytokines as potential therapeutic targets is required.

Cytokines are important drivers in liver inflammation and may contribute to tissue injury . The cytokine profile of our experimental groups was a mixed phenotype representing both a Th2 and Th17 response consisting of IL-13 and IL-17 with biliary damage induced by pathogenic cholangiocyte-specific T cells. Although it is conventionally thought that IL-13 and IL-17 are mutually regulated, this cytokine profile was exaggerated in obese animals showing that both Th2 and Th17 responses may co-exist , . In our model it is possible that numerous cytokines are acting synergistically to cause a more severe phenotype of experimental PSC. Interestingly, attenuation of GI tract diseases has been reported in the absence of either cytokine , . It is tempting to speculate that an IL-13 + IL-17 + double positive T helper subpopulation with enhanced pathogenicity emerges during biliary injury in obese animals. Studies addressing this possibility are currently taking place in our laboratory. We also found higher levels of IL-9 in obese mice suggesting that IL-9 may be acting as an additional factor given this Th2-like cytokine has been found to promote inflammation in the GI tract – .

Interestingly, levels of IL-1α inversely correlated with obesity and biliary injury and as disease severity increased, IL-1α levels tended to decrease. A clear explanation for this phenomenon remains controversial as IL-1α is thought to display similar inflammatory features to IL-1β and conflicting reports show a positive relationship between obesity and IL-1α , while others show an inverse relationship or no clear correlation , . When we neutralized IL-15, levels of IL-1α were restored and this was associated with attenuated cholangitis.

Macrophages have been described as a key cell type potentially contributing to both the promotion and resolution of liver inflammation and tissue injury. One paradigm stratifies macrophages based on Ly6C expression where Ly6C hi macrophages may promote inflammation in early stages whereas Ly6C lo occur later and may limit inflammation , . Although we observed diminished numbers of the latter population in early phase of disease, non-obese mice were able to recover Ly6C lo macrophages in the later phase of disease while obese mice did not recover this Ly6C lo macrophage population even when Ly6C hi F4/80 + cells were not significantly affected. This suggests that macrophage proliferation rather than infiltration may be responsible for the inability to recover putative restorative Ly6C lo macrophages. Critically, blocking of IL-15 resulted in the reappearance of Ly6C lo macrophages in the liver tissue of obese mice and the number of Ly6C lo macrophages in obese mice surpassed the number of Ly6C lo macrophages in non-obese animals suggesting that in absence of IL-15 infiltrating macrophages are able to rapidly transition into restorative Ly6C lo macrophages.

Although we did not observe any fibrosis in this model of PSC, obese mice exhibited enhanced expression of TIMP-1, a pro-fibrotic gene emerging as a consequence of obesity , and promoted by IL-13 and IL-17 , as well as high levels of pro-fibrotic chemokines such as CCL3 and CCL5 – . A role for CCR5 + neutrophils sequestering CCL3 and CCL5 during the resolution phase of inflammation has been shown to support decreased fibrosis and a return to homeostasis . Interestingly, in this current study the mice with obesity and cholangitis were found to have predominately CCL5 − neutrophils in the liver as well as higher serum levels of CCL3 and CCL5. This data suggests that the onset of fibrosis in PSC during obesity may in part be influenced by the balance between pro-inflammatory and pro-resolution neutrophils. Therefore, future studies longer in duration will evaluate the potential of accelerated fibrosis in obese animals following a strong inflammatory reaction.

In summary, diet-induced obesity results in the reduced presence of tolerogenic-like cell populations in the liver. This in turn prevents the suppression of subsequent inflammatory challenges and primes cells to over-produce IL-15. Higher levels of IL-15 subsequently exaggerates severity in our murine model of antigen-driven liver disease. As our knowledge of PSC continues to develop there is potential to generate novel mouse models that may enhance our understanding of this chronic, immune-mediated disease. Future studies evaluating the potential to neutralize the detrimental effects of cytokines such as IL-15 may represent a novel treatment strategy for patients with PSC.

sections.abstract:
Postoperative neurocognitive disorder (PND) is characterized by cognitive deficits that emerge after surgery. Although often reversible within weeks or months, PND can persist and lead to significant central dysfunction and an increased risk of dementia. Given that obesity is a chronic low-grade inflammatory condition previously associated with structural and functional brain alterations, we hypothesized and demonstrated that it could be a significant risk factor for PND.

We assessed the incidence of PND and cognitive performance in obese individuals undergoing cardiac or orthopedic surgeries. In parallel, we developed a preclinical model combining diet-induced obesity in mice with surgically induced tibial fracture. Pharmacological (ketoprofen), surgical (adipose tissue ablation), and behavioral (calorie restriction) interventions were used to target obesity-associated inflammation.

Compared with nonobese individuals, obese patients presented a greater incidence of early postoperative cognitive changes and lower cognitive performance ( p < 0.009). In mice, the combination of obesity and surgery results in exacerbated signs of PND. Importantly, obesity-related PND in mice was prevented by interventions that reduced central and systemic inflammation.

These findings identify obesity-driven fat mass and inflammation as strong risk factors for PND for the first time. Targeting obesity-associated inflammatory mechanisms may represent an effective strategy to reduce the incidence of this debilitating postoperative condition.

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-026-08629-6 .
sections.other:
Obesity has heavily impacted society worldwide, as it has progressively become a major public health concern. This burden is not only due to an association with metabolic disorders [, ] but also because of various comorbidities and complications, such as cardiovascular diseases [], cancer [] and brain alterations []. In addition to metabolic consequences, obesity has been recognized as a driver of cognitive impairments in both rodents [] and humans [, ] and a reduction in brain volume. Notably, a particularly deleterious impact of obesity has been reported regarding the hippocampus, a key brain structure that supports cognition and memory [, ]. Among the underlying mechanisms for these central defects are changes in cellular and endocrine functions observed with excessive adipose tissue development that lead to systemic low-grade inflammation [, ], alterations in the blood‒brain barrier (BBB) [, ], microglial activation [] and neuroinflammation [], which are associated with alterations in cognitive pathways [, ].

Surgery is associated with cognitive changes, named perioperative neurocognitive disorders []. Whereas surgery-induced postoperative delirium (POD) is a short-term alteration of consciousness that can be rapidly reversed (hours to a few days), more prolonged and persistent postoperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) marked by alterations in learning, memory, attention and executive functions, similar to those observed in dementia, can occur [, ]. Prolonged PNDs are poorly characterized and are diagnosed only by comparisons of pre- and postsurgical cognitive performance. However, PND has been closely linked with advanced age [, ] and low preoperative cognitive reserve [–] and is associated with an unbalanced inflammatory response after surgery [–], leading to alterations in the BBB and microglial overactivation [, ] and consequently neuronal alterations [, ].

Other risk factors, such as diabetes, have been linked to PND development in both humans [, ] and rodents [], indicating the potential role of dysregulated metabolism at PND onset. However, in the context of metabolic impairment, little is known about the synergistic effect of well-described obesity-related inflammation on the development of PND. Taken together, these observations suggest that obesity-related low-grade inflammation could represent a major risk factor for PND, which is potentially mediated by alterations in adipose tissue. Thus, gaining deeper insight into and specifically targeting the role of adipose tissue in obesity-associated PND may represent an innovative and novel preventive and/or therapeutic strategy.

Here, we demonstrated that obesity per se is directly associated with the development of early postoperative cognitive changes in humans and mice, with a potential link to the inflammatory status of adipose tissue. By combining obesity and invasive surgery in mice, we demonstrated that obesity-associated PND is mediated by both an increase in BBB permeability and an imbalance of glial cells, which specifically leads to functional declines associated with neuron-altered activation and transmission of information. Notably, subcutaneous adipose tissue near the site of surgery was crucial for the onset of PND in obese mice. In this context, reversing obesity features via a nutritional approach considerably reduces the incidence of PND in mice, paving the way for a preventive strategy potentially translatable to humans.

Our human study examines males and females, and similar findings are reported for both sexes, as expected from the literature. Our study examined male mice because male animals exhibit less variability in phenotype, and the available literature demonstrates an increase in PND occurrence specifically in males compared with females.

The Impact of Obesity on Postoperative Cognitive Dysfunction: The Role of Adipose Tissue Study (ODCOTA) was conducted as an observational, prospective, monocentric, longitudinal study in the cardiovascular and orthopedic surgery departments of the Toulouse University Hospital. This work was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki principles and approved by the local research ethics committee (Comité d’éthique pour la recherche du CHU de Toulouse no.NTC04907565) in 2021. An a priori sample size calculation was performed on the basis of previously published data [, ], in which the incidence of postoperative delirium in the lean group was 0.25 and 0.50 in the obese group. Using these estimates, a power of 80%, a two-sided alpha risk of 0.05, and an assumed incidence of 0.25 in the lean group and 0.50 in the obese group, we obtained a required sample size of n = 57 per group. To account for potential missing data or incomplete variables in the final analysis, we planned to include additional patients in the study. Patients were enrolled in the study between October 2021 and February 2023 and were followed at 6 months after surgery. Patients with a body mass index (BMI) between 18.5 and 25 kg/m 2 were included in the lean group, and patients with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 were assigned to the obese group. All patients were 60 years or older and were undergoing planned surgery. The exclusion criteria included urgent surgeries, patients with a Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) score < 20 or preoperative cognitive disorders.

The primary endpoint was the occurrence of postoperative cognitive changes, which were defined as delirium and/or PND. The presence of delirium was verified daily. Trained research personnel, including nurses, assessed the presence of PND. The occurrence of delirium was evaluated via the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) adapted for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) test, which is used when a patient is admitted to our intensive care unit. The main criteria were as follows: sudden onset, inattention, disorganized thoughts, alterations in the level of consciousness, and associated criteria (disorientation, memory loss, abnormal perception, psychomotor disorders, and sleep–wake disorders). If any of these indicators were present, the patient was scored as delirious. Patients were assessed during the first seven days after surgery. The duration of delirium was calculated as the number of days between the initial positive delirium assessment and the final positive delirium assessment.

The presence of PND was evaluated by assessing changes in cognitive function one day before surgery (baseline) and five days after surgery by medically trained personnel. We choose the MMSE for patients who underwent cardiac surgery and the TICS (Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status) for those who underwent orthopedic surgery as measures of cognitive function because they are commonly used in geriatric patients and have been used to diagnose PND. After surgery, MMSE and TICS evaluations were performed on day 5. Patients were classified with PND at discharge when they experienced a decline in percentage evolution:

This calculation was applied identically for patients assessed with the MMSE and with the TICS. Given that the TICS is a telephone adaptation of the MMSE assessing the same cognitive domains (memory, orientation, calculation, language), both scores are directly comparable in terms of percentage change.

Finally, we attempted to identify the risk factors for PND in the population via biological sample analysis. To do so, blood was collected on the day of surgery and the day after surgery. Subcutaneous adipose tissue was also collected at the site of surgery.

All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines for animal studies and were approved by an ethics committee (US006/CREFRE Oncopole 23-3U1301-CD-05). C57BL6/J WT male mice at 8 weeks of age were obtained from Janvier Laboratory (St-Berthevin, France). The mice were randomly assigned to groups. The mice were housed conventionally at a constant temperature (20–22 °C) and humidity (50–60%) in the animal room, with a 12–12 h light–dark cycle and free access to food and water. The animals were fed standard rodent chow (normal diet from SAFE A04) or a HFD with 60% calories from fat (Research Diet D12492) for 12 weeks. The number of animals used for the behavior test was calculated via G*Power analysis.

Unilateral closed tibial fracture was performed under 2% sevoflurane (Abbott, Suresnes France) anesthesia and buprenorphine (Buprecare code 2145464, 100 μg/kg) as an analgesic as previously described. All the mice (lean and obese) were exposed to the same level of drugs on the basis of their weight. Briefly, a closed fracture of the right hind paw was produced via a specially designed fracture apparatus (blunt guillotine). Before fracture, intramedullary pinning was performed under sterile conditions; a hole was made percutaneously above the tibial tuberosity via a 27-gauge needle (BD® Microlance − 27 G 3⁄4 L 19 mm). The needle was then directed into the medullary canal. By rotating the needle, the canal was reamed 5 mm up to the ankle joint. The end of the needle was cut as short as possible so that the skin could roll over and cover it. No sutures were used. The mouse was then placed with the leg on the anvil so that the blunt guillotine lined up with the proximal third of the tibia. The weight of 300 g was dropped from a height of 10 cm to fracture the tibia shaft. Closed fracture was confirmed postmortem by examining whether the nail was intramedullary or not and whether the bone fractured.

ND- and HFD-fed mice were injected intraperitoneally with NaCl or 50 mg/kg ketoprofen 1 h prior to tibial fracture and 24 h after fracture.

The subcutaneous adipose tissue of obese mice was surgically removed to determine the role of specific depots of adipose tissue in PND development. In one group of mice, the right subcutaneous adipose tissue (abli), which was ipsilateral to the fracture, was ablated, whereas in the other group, the left adipose tissue (ablc), which was contralateral to the fracture, was removed. Briefly, the animals were anesthetized with 2% sevoflurane (Abbott, Suresnes, France). The paw was then shaved to ensure a clean surgical zone. The adipose tissue was ablated, and buprenorphine (100 μg/kg) was used as an analgesic. The mice were subsequently weighed every day for two weeks.

C57BL6/J WT mice at 8 weeks of age were obtained from Janvier Laboratory (St-Berthevin, France) and were fed a HFD with 60% calories from fat (Research Diet) for 8 weeks. The mice were then switched to standard ad libitum rodent chow (a normal diet) for an additional 4 weeks to induce calorie restriction.

The mice were fasted overnight before the test. Briefly, glycemia was measured with a glucometer (Glucocheck, Roche, France) before and after oral administration of a 60% glucose solution (3 g of glucose per kg of weight). The results are expressed as areas under the curve.

Blood was collected in heparin-coated tubes and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4 °C, after which the plasma phase was collected and stored at −80 °C until use. Metabolic parameters were measured with an ELISA kit for insulin (Alpco-Eurobio Scientifics 80-INSMU-E10) and colorimetric kits for free glycerol and free fatty acids (Sigma F6428).

Behavioral experiments were performed during the first half of the light phase, and the data were scored by two independent scorers.

Fear conditioning allows one to measure hippocampus-dependent memory of the association of a shock to a context (contextual fear conditioning (CFC)) and the memory of the association of the shock to an auditory cue, which does not involve the hippocampus. On the first day, the mice were placed in the conditioned context (Noldus EthoVision) for 150 seconds. Then, a sound cue (75–80 Db, 7 kHz, 30 s) was emitted, ending with an electric shock (0.75 mA, 2 last seconds of the sound cue) delivered by a grid floor. The tone and foot‒shock pairings were repeated with an intertrial interval of 60 s, followed by 30 s of exploration before the mouse was taken back to its home cage. The next day, fear is evaluated by measuring freezing behavior, which is defined as the complete absence of every movement except respiration. It was first measured while the mice were placed in the conditioned context for 4 minutes to assess contextual memory. One hour and a half later, the mice were placed in an alternative context for 2 min, followed by two more minutes with the sound cue to assess tone fear memory. All apparatuses and testing chambers were cleaned with 70% ethanol between each animal. The results are expressed as the percentage of freezing in the recall phase. The experimental settings, adapted from Sayegh et al [] were chosen to allow us to obtain similar and high freezing rates for both the context and the sound cue.

The 7-trial social memory test, adapted from Rey et al. [], is based on the fact that social interaction with unfamiliar mice decreases when the mouse becomes familiar. The habituation of the exploration of a conspecific can thus be considered a measure of social memory. Each mouse was placed in a large chamber (25 × 35 cm) for a 10-min habituation period, with an empty cylindrical small cage placed in the center (8 cm diameter). A stimulus unfamiliar mouse, also C57BL6/J from the same sex but never encountered before, was subsequently introduced into the small cage for six successive trials of 5 min (interval of 10 min without mice between every trial). In the seventh trial, a novel stimulus unfamiliar with a mouse was introduced to measure social learning. The next day, the mice were placed in the chamber again, with the first stimulus mouse used to recall social memory. The direct interactions between the tested mouse and the stimulus mouse were scored manually by the experimenter. The results are expressed as a percentage of the investigation time compared with the first trial in each group. All apparatuses and testing chambers were cleaned with 70% ethanol between each animal.

An object location test measures spatial memory. It evaluates the ability of a mouse to discriminate between a novel and a familiar spatial location measure. Each mouse was first placed in an open field with a visual cue (striped pattern) for 10 minutes of habituation without objects. After 1 hour, during acquisition, two identical objects were placed in the middle of the open field. The mice were allowed to explore for 10 min, during which the time spent exploring the two objects was recorded. The next day, the test phase was performed by placing the mouse back in the same open field where one of the two objects had been moved to a novel location. The position (left or right) of the displaced object was chosen according to the preference of the mouse during acquisition pseudo randomly to reduce bias toward a particular position. The mice were allowed to explore the objects for 10 min. The direct interactions were scored manually by the experimenter. The percentage of interaction was calculated as follows: time exploring the displaced object/total time exploring * 100. A preference index above 50% indicates a preference for the displaced object, and 50% indicates no preference (random choice). All apparatuses and testing chambers were cleaned with 70% ethanol between each animal.

Automatic analysis of locomotion in the center and periphery of the open field (Noldus EthoVision) during the habituation phase also allowed measurements of locomotion and anxiety.

Mechanical allodynia was assessed on the right hind paws of the mice. Each mouse was placed in the von Frey chamber for 30 minutes of habituation. Three filaments were used: 0.16, 0.6 and 1.2 g. The filament was applied on the plantar zone with enough force to cause the filament to bend and remain in contact for a total of 3 seconds. Each filament was tested 5 times with at least 5 minutes between each stimulation. If no withdrawal response was observed, the next highest filament was tested. The withdrawal response is characterized by triphasic paw retraction or paw licking. Animals were tested before surgery and at 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 3 days and 7 days post-surgery, with each animal serving as its own control. All apparatuses and testing chambers were cleaned with 70% ethanol between each animal.

The kinetic weight bearing (KWB) system is based on footprint tracking in spontaneously moving animals. Parameters such as the maximum force (mN), mass velocity (N/s), speed, cadence, and step patterns are processed while the mouse walks in a corridor with sensors. Each mouse was placed in the KWB apparatus 5 successive times before surgery and at 3 days post-surgery, with each mouse acting as its own control. All apparatuses and testing chambers were cleaned with 70% ethanol between each animal.

The animals were euthanized via intracardiac PBS perfusion under general anesthesia with 2% sevoflurane (Abbott, Suresnes, France) and exsanguinated. Biological samples of blood, brain or hippocampus; surgical hematoma; and white adipose tissue (visceral and subcutaneous) were collected for analysis.

Total RNA (1 μg) was isolated from the site of surgery hematoma, adipocytes, the adipose tissue, and the hippocampus. Tissues were lysed in Qiazol (Qiagen), and RNA was extracted via a GeneJet RNA Purification Kit (K0732, Fermentas, Thermo Scientific). The RNA was reverse transcribed via random hexamers, dNTPs, buffer and Superscript II reverse transcriptase (MultiScribe, Applied Biosystems) via a Thermocycler T3000® (Applied Biosystems®). Real-time PCR was performed with both sense and antisense oligonucleotides in a final volume of 10 µl in a 384-well plate via SYBR Green universal PCR master mix (Eurogentec) on Via7 (Applied Biosystems®). Analysis of 36B4/Hprt/B2-microglobulin mRNA was performed to normalize gene expression (Eurogentec®), which was expressed as an arbitrary unit (A.U.).

Hippocampal lysates were generated via the use of RIPA lysis buffer and a complete inhibitor cocktail from Roche Diagnostics (Indianapolis, IN, USA) and a phosphatase inhibitor cocktail from Thermo Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). Protein dosage was determined via the Lowry technique (Thermo Scientific; 10677904). The lysates were boiled in Laemmli buffer and separated via SDS‒PAGE on a 4‒12% acrylamide gel. Proteins were then transferred onto a nitrocellulose membrane. The membranes were blocked with 5% BSA in TBST containing 0.1% Tween and incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. The membranes were incubated with rabbit peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature. Immunoreactive proteins were detected via the Clarity Western ECL Substrate (Bio-Rad) and quantified via Image Lab software (Bio-Rad). The data were normalized to those of the GAPDH control.

BBB disruption was investigated via Evans blue dye (EB; Sigma‒Aldrich, E2129) extravasation methods. EB (2%) was prepared in PBS and filtered to remove particles. The animals were anesthetized during all the procedures. Briefly, 4 mL/kg diluted EB was retro-orbitally injected and allowed to circulate for 1 h. Mice were perfused with 15 mL of PBS, and the brains were isolated immediately. For quantitative measurement, the brains were homogenized in 500 µL of formamide (Sigma‒Aldrich). The samples were incubated at 55 °C for 24 h to extract the EB from the brain tissue. The samples were subsequently centrifuged, the supernatants containing formamide were collected, and the absorbance of the supernatants was measured at 610 nm via Varioskan. The results are expressed as the amount of EB (ng) per tissue amount (mg).

Brain and adipose tissues were collected for histological studies. The animals were anesthetized and euthanized via intracardiac perfusion with PBS. The brain and adipose tissues were collected and placed in 10% formalin (Sigma‒Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA; HT501128). The brains were left for 72 h at 4 °C and transferred into 30% sucrose solution for one week. The brains were frozen in isopentane at −80 °C and stored until sectioning. A cryostat was used to obtain 30 µm sections. Primary antibodies were used at 1:500 overnight at 4 °C, and secondary antibodies were used at 1:1000 for one hour at RT. The slides were mounted with Fluoroshield with DAPI mounting medium.

The adipose tissue was left for 48 h at 4 °C and then transferred to 70% ethanol. The samples were dehydrated in sequential alcohol baths (30%, 50%, 75%, 100%), washed with histoclear solution, and then embedded in paraffin. A Vibroslice was used to obtain 7 µm sections. Adipose tissue slides were subjected to hematoxylin (Sigma; 51275) staining. The slides were mounted with Eukit medium. Acquisitions were performed on a Nanozoomer scanner (Hamamatsu Photonics, Hamamatsu City, Japan). Image quantification was performed via ImageJ freeware (National Institutes of Health, USA).

Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analyses were performed after PBS perfusion. Forebrains, the site-of-surgery hematomas and white adipose tissue were collected. Fresh forebrains were rapidly dissected and manually homogenized. The homogenates were passed through a 70 µm cell strainer (BD Biosciences), and the centrifuged supernatants were removed and discarded. The pellet was resuspended for Percoll gradient separation, with the myelin and top phases discarded. Site-of-surgery hematomas were incubated with Liberase and BSA solutions for 20 minutes at 37 °C and manually homogenized. The homogenates were passed through a 70 µm cell strainer (BD Biosciences), and the centrifuged supernatants were removed and discarded. The white adipose tissue was incubated with collagenase A and BSA for 45 minutes at 37 °C and filtered through 150 µm. Adipocytes were collected at the top phase, and the stromal vascular fraction was collected at the bottom. After being washed with PBS, the cells were exposed to dead cell stains. Then, the samples were blocked with anti-mouse CD16/CD32 (1/100, BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) and incubated with an antibody mixture diluted in PBS. The fluorescent cells were immediately identified via a flow cytometer (BD LSR Fortessa) and analyzed via Kaluza software.

The gating strategy was performed as follows:

The plasma cytokine concentrations were determined via a Simple Plex TM Assay (ProteinSimple, CA, USA) on the Ella TM instrument according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A panel of four cytokines, namely, CXCL-10, IL-1β, IL-6 and TNFα, was used on a preskit cartridge. Ella™ was calibrated via the in-cartridge factory standard curve. All samples were measured after a 1:2 dilution. The cartridge was inserted into the Ella TM device for 70 minutes. The concentrations are expressed in pg/mL. All the samples were assayed in triplicate.

The data are presented as the means ± SEMs. For the human cohort, the data were analyzed via descriptive statistics for the lean vs. obese groups and the absence of PND vs. PND via the Mann‒Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Variables with p < 0.1 in the univariate model without PND vs. PND were retained as candidates for inclusion in the multivariate model and were entered, simultaneously adjusting for all of them. The associations between different covariates and dependent variables were calculated via multivariate analysis, with an initial threshold set at a p value of <0.05. After the exclusion of collinear covariates, stepwise regression (backward elimination) was applied, starting with all the variables initially chosen and then progressively removing non-significant ones. We only retained parameters that remained statistically significant in the multivariate model (e.g., p < 0.05) after mutual adjustment. Model performance was evaluated using the Hosmer-Lemeshow test for calibration, the AUC for discrimination, and the proportion of correctly classified patients for overall classification accuracy. For comparisons of the two independent variables (diet (ND/HFD) and surgery (no fracture/ fracture)), we performed two-way ANOVA followed by four pairwise Student’s t -tests with a Tukey post-hoc correction. For social interaction trials, each trial was normalized to the 1st trial for each group and each trial was compared to the baseline using one-sample T-test. For object location groups the groups were compared with a one-sample T-test compared to 50%. For comparison of two groups a Student’s 2-sided t -test was used. p values less than 0.05 (* or #), 0.01 (** or ##) or 0.001 (*** or ###) or (**** or ####) were considered statistically significant. # is used for comparison to control diet. Analysis was performed on GraphPad software.

This human study was approved by the research ethics board (protocol number RC31/21/0014), and oral informed consent was obtained from each patient (RIPH 2G). This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04907565 dated May 2021). All experimental procedures involving animals were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines for animal studies and were approved by an ethics committee (US006/CREFRE Oncopole 23-3U1301-CD-05).
sections.results:
Previous metadata analysis of the relationship between obesity and PND did not reveal a clear association [], possibly due to heterogeneity among the inclusion criteria and/or overall study design. In this study, we compared lean and obese individuals with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 who had undergone cardiac ( n = 69) or orthopedic surgery ( n = 37), excluding all patients with preoperative cognitive alterations (MMSE < 20) (Supplemental Figure ). Cognitive functions were assessed pre- and postoperatively via cognitive tests and biological sampling (see section “”). While patients with obesity had a greater BMI (33.2 kg/m 2 vs. 23.3 kg/m 2 , p < 0.0001) and presented with obesity-associated metabolic alterations, such as hypertension ( p < 0.0001) and diabetes ( p < 0.004), age, sex and surgery type were evenly distributed across the groups (Supplemental Tables and ). The main criterion for study was the occurrence of postoperative cognitive changes, such as post-operative delirium (POD) and/or PND. Compared with lean patients, obese patients presented lower cognitive performance ( p < 0.009) not attributable to delirium ( p < 0.49) but rather only to the percentage of decline in PND ( p = 0.0001) (Table ). Moreover, regarding the occurrence of neurocognitive disorders, obesity but also type 2 diabetes and anti-diabetic drugs, pre-operative anti-depressant, ketamine, intra-operative parameters and delirium appeared to be significantly increased in the patients who developed neurocognitive disorder after surgery (Table ). Thus, we tested all those parameters in a multivariate model to identify their risk associated with PND. Among all those parameters, only obesity appeared to be a strong risk factor for PND, as determined by multivariate analysis (OR 7.26, 95% CI (2.08–25.33), p = 0.002), together with POD and ketamine, as previously described [, ] (Table ). These findings highlight obesity as a major driver of early postoperative cognitive changes during surgery.

We next wished to model PND in mice. To do so, we first induced obesity in C57BL6/j male mice by feeding them a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks, which resulted in all the hallmarks of obesity in terms of excess body weight and adipose tissue mass [] (Supplemental Figure A-H), systemic and adipose tissue inflammation [] (Supplemental Figure I-K), and impaired glucose homeostasis and metabolism (Supplemental Figure L-R). We then surgically induced a tibial fracture as described by Minville et al []. The day after surgery, mice were subjected to a battery of hippocampus-dependent memory tests, including contextual fear conditioning (CFC), object location (OL), and social memory test (SMT), to evaluate their cognitive performance (Fig. A). In the CFC test, mice learn to associate a specific context with an aversive stimulus; memory is assessed by measuring freezing behavior upon re-exposure to the same context. In the OL test, which relies on spatial memory, mice are exposed to two identical objects and, after a delay, one object is displaced, intact memory is reflected by a preference for exploring the relocated object. In the SMT, mice are exposed to a conspecific and memory is evaluated based on their ability to discriminate between familiar and novel individuals, reflecting social recognition memory. We found that, compared with ND mice, surgery impaired performance in these hippocampus-dependent tasks, with more pronounced deficits in obese mice. Specifically, HFD mice exhibited reduced freezing in the CFC test, indicating impaired contextual memory (Fig. B), failed to preferentially explore the displaced object in the OL test (Fig. C), and showed reduced social discrimination, indicative of impaired learning and recall in the SMT (Fig. D). Interestingly, hippocampus-independent memory, assessed using the cued fear conditioning test, did not show any differences between WT and HFD mice after surgery (Supplemental Figure A). This highlights the specificity of the surgical impact on hippocampus-dependent memory alterations observed in PND. Moreover, other parameters that could explain the increased incidence of PND in HFD mice after surgery remained unchanged when comparing obese and lean mice. Indeed, pain, measured by withdrawal responses in the von Frey test, increased similarly in both groups 1 hour after surgery and returned to baseline within 1 day (Supplemental Figure B). Similarly, locomotor activity, assessed by both total distance traveled and velocity, was affected by the HFD diet but not by surgery (Supplemental Figure C–D). In addition, detailed movement analysis using the KWB did not reveal any differences between lean and obese mice after surgery (Supplemental Figure E). Finally, anxiety does not appear to contribute to the observed cognitive dysfunction (Supplemental Figure F).

Direct analysis of the hippocampus revealed that only obese mice presented significant decreases in the neuronal markers NeuN [] and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Fig. A–C). While the decrease in BDNF expression persisted over time, the change in NeuN expression was transient, with a return to the basal level by 24 hours as shown by the NeuN quantification by histology and flow cytometry (Fig. D–F and Supplemental Figure A-I). This transient decrease points to impaired neuronal activation and not to neuronal cell death, as already mentioned []. Moreover, HFD-fed mice specifically presented lower expression of postsynaptic genes responsible for memory storage and recall [], including Creb, Arc, Bdnf and Fos , after fracture (Fig. G). Finally, tibial fracture also induced a significant decrease in the number of PSA-Ncam-positive cells within the hippocampus, a learning and synapse remodeling marker [], and associated gene dysfunction, particularly in HFD-fed mice (Fig. H–K). Notably, without fracture, HFD-fed mice did not display alterations in any of these cognition markers (Supplemental Figure J-M). Together, these results indicate that obese mice specifically display greater sensitivity after tibial fracture vi a altered neuronal activation and impaired plasticity.

Tibial fracture-induced PND is driven by an unbalanced acute inflammatory process that begins at the injury site and then spreads systemically to the central nervous system [, ]. We confirmed the critical role of inflammation in obesity-associated PND development by treating mice perioperatively with the anti-inflammatory agent ketoprofen, similar to the effects observed postoperatively in treated aged rats []. Ketoprofen treatment restored cognitive function in obese mice after surgery in the OL test (Supplemental Figure A) by improving systemic inflammation (Supplemental Figure B), cognitive markers (Supplemental Figure G-K) and local inflammation at the site of surgery (Supplemental Figure L).

The role of activated glial cells, including microglia and astrocytes, in obesity and PND has been previously reported [, ]. Indeed, microglia play a key role in neuroinflammation as the brain’s first line of defense [], whereas astrocyte activation, known as astrogliosis, is a secondary pathway involved in the well-documented unbalance of central inflammation [, ]. In the basal state, obesity promotes microglial overactivation, as evaluated by IBA-1 (ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1) hippocampal protein expression and an associated decrease in GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein), an astrocyte activation marker (Supplemental Figure A). Interestingly, 72 h after fracture, this regulation was completely reversed since obese mice presented a significant decrease in IBA-1 and an associated increase in hippocampal GFAP (Fig. A–C). The long-term (24 h) surgery-induced increase in GFAP expression, together with the blunted expression of IBA-1, may suggest that astrogliosis is specifically involved in obese mice due to failure of the central immune response. No changes in the number of Iba1-positive or CD45 low /CD11b-positive microglia and in the number of GFAP- or ACSA2-positive astrocytes were observed under any condition (Supplemental Figure B-H). Thus, we hypothesized that even if obese mice display basal microglial overactivation, after surgery, these cells may not be further activated or may present phenotypic and metabolic changes that impair their response, leading to astrogliosis. To fully understand this phenomenon, a deeper phenotypic characterization of microglia and astrocytes is needed.

Moreover, we found an increased BBB permeability in obese mice after surgery (Fig. D), which is known to facilitate central inflammation [], with lower expression of the tight junction proteins occludin and zonula occludens 1 (ZO1) but not claudin 5 (Fig. E and Supplemental Figure I). Systemic inflammation was also increased by surgery, especially in obese animals, as the levels of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β were elevated, whereas the level of the chemokine CXCL-10 was reduced (Fig. G–I). At the site of surgery, the hematomas collected from ND- and HFD-fed mice, which were mostly composed of red blood cells and a small proportion of immune cells [], were composed of the same proportions of CD45-positive immune cells (Supplemental Figure J). However, the expression of the proinflammatory macrophage marker CD86 was greater in the HFD + surgery group than in the control group (Fig. J). Moreover, qualitative assessment of the inflammatory profile of immune cells via flow cytometry and gene expression analyses revealed that hematomas from obese mice exhibited a more pronounced inflammatory state (Fig. K–L). Together, these data suggest that there is an elevated local and systemic proinflammatory response in obese mice, possibly priming central alterations and PND.

To validate the causative role of obesity in PND development, we placed obese mice on a calorie restriction (CR) regimen. CR is known to have beneficial effects on weight, adiposity, metabolic parameters and cognition [, ]. After 8 weeks of HFD feeding, obese mice were fed a normal diet for 4 weeks. As expected, this induced a significant reduction in whole-body and adipose tissue weights and gene expression (Supplemental Figure A-D). Strikingly, calorie restriction restored cognition after surgery, as measured by both the OL and SMT tests (Fig. A–C), and maintained NeuN and BDNF expression (Fig. D–F and Supplemental Figure E-F), together with a lower degree of inflammation at the site of surgery, as evidenced by greater expression of IL-10 (Supplemental Figure G). These results highlight the potential translation of our findings to the clinic, as they suggest that modifications of the diet before invasive surgery may be a preventive strategy for obesity-induced PND. However, obesity is associated with multiple changes that could promote the onset of PND. First, we found that obesity-associated metabolic homeostatic defects do not appear to be involved in the observed induction of PND shortly after surgery since no major change in metabolism was observed after 4 weeks of calorie restriction (Supplemental Figure A-E). Thus, we hypothesized that obesity might play a role by itself through a change in white adipose tissue, as obesity-induced modifications in adipose tissue are widely known []. Interestingly, surgery did not impact whole-body weight or the weights of the visceral or subcutaneous ipsilateral or contralateral adipose tissue depots (Supplemental Figure F-I). Even so, unlike the other depots, the subcutaneous ipsilateral (SCi) adipose tissue presented altered responses in genes related to adipogenesis, such as FAS, PPARγ, CEPBα and LHS (Supplemental Figure J-O), and immune cells, measured by flow cytometry with the recruitment of neutrophils and a reduction in lymphocytes (B, T and NK) in the stroma-vascular fraction of the adipose tissue after tibial fracture (Supplemental Figure P-Q), suggesting that the SCi undergoes a specific alteration in response to such invasive surgery. Nevertheless, it is important to note that both ND- and HFD-fed mice presented with alterations in the SCi in response to surgery. However, the data suggest that, owing to preexisting modifications in the adipose tissue that occur with HFD feeding, the SCi of obese mice respond differently to surgery, leading to the onset of PND.

To validate the specific involvement of the SCi in obesity-induced PND, we subjected obese mice to surgical ablation of the SCi or the contralateral adipose tissue after 12 weeks of HFD feeding. Ablation did not affect whole-body weight or the adipose tissue weights of the visceral depot or the subcutaneous contralateral depot (Supplemental Figure A-C). Remarkably, we found that the specific absence of SCi adipose tissue in obese animals prevented the induction of PND, whereas the removal of subcutaneous contralateral adipose tissue did not affect the OL or SMT (Fig. A-C). This prevention of PND by SCi ablation was associated with greater expression of NeuN in the hippocampi of the mice than was SC contralateral ablation, while there was no statistically significant difference in BDNF after surgery in either group (Fig. D–F, Supplemental Figure E-F). This unexpected result highlights the critical and overlooked role of the local role of subcutaneous adipose tissue and the inflammatory preoperative environment in PND occurrence.
sections.discussion:
This study provides the first direct evidence across clinical and preclinical models that obesity is an independent risk factor for early postoperative cognitive changes development, with a direct link to the excess of adipose tissue and its localization and inflammation. Our human cohort analysis indicated that a loss of cognitive capacity after surgery occurs primarily in obese patients who have undergone either cardiovascular or orthopedic surgeries, which are two surgeries with a known high risk for PND []. This alteration does not seem to be the consequence of postoperative delirium. These results confirm the findings of a recent clinical study that characterized obesity as a risk factor for PND, among other metabolic impairments, such as metabolic syndrome or elevated HDL-C plasma levels []. Even if further studies with larger cohort sizes, later cognitive assessments to identify prolonged PND and more specific tests, such as verbal learning tests, color-word tests, letter digit span tests and the MoCA, are needed to confirm this association. The presented results highlight patient BMI as a crucial preoperative consideration regarding the risk of invasive surgery on cognitive capacity in the postoperative period. Moreover, while we identified differences in the adipose tissue inflammatory profile between obese patients and lean patients, no associations with PND were detected (data not shown). This can be explained by the low number of patients and deeper analysis of the adipose tissue sampled and the blood with markers of inflammation and neurodegeneration, such as NfL, which could strengthen our findings. Consequently, a better characterization of the link between obesity and its association with the onset of PND is needed. To address this limitation, we used a diet-induced obesity mouse model together with tibial fracture to demonstrate that obesity represents an important contribution to alterations in hippocampal-associated memory, as evaluated by various cognitive tests. This effect does not appear to be due to the well-described obesity-related hyperalgesia, anxiety [, ] and/or fracture-induced locomotor defects. Our results are in accordance with those of a previous study that showed that both aging and obesity are associated with a greater incidence of PND in mice []. In addition, we found that PND was characterized by defects in neuronal activity and synaptic plasticity based on decreased expression of NeuN, BDNF and PSA-Ncam in the hippocampus of obese mice with tibial fractures. As lower expression of PSA-Ncam could also be associated with immature neurons, further experiments investigating neurogenesis should be performed via doublecortin (DCX) staining of dividing neurons in the dentate gyrus.

Another aspect of PND that we found to be strongly associated with this condition is inflammation. Among the potential targets involved in an exacerbated inflammatory response in obese mice, we first focused our attention on the brain. Despite basal microglia-primed activation, obese mice do not display stronger microglial reactivity after fracture. Even if we cannot rule out a priming effect of obesity on central structures, this unexpected result may suggest that, as already shown by the Wyss-Coray team [], cells in a highly inflammatory environment are prone to phenotypic changes that act to maintain the unbalanced inflammation. Further experiments are needed to definitively validate this hypothesis in the context of obesity-associated surgery. On the other hand, the observed increase in the astrocyte response to surgery strongly suggests that unbalanced inflammation occurs due to a lack of, or a maladapted, response by microglia []. This hypothesis is reinforced by the increased permeability of the BBB, which has been previously tightly associated with instances of neuroinflammation []. As previously reported in other contexts [], we hypothesized that such central responses may arise due to inflammation in the periphery, as only obese-fractured mice presented an increase in systemic inflammatory cytokines that was prevented by ketoprofen treatment. Additionally, hematomas collected from the site of surgery in obese mice presented a stronger inflammatory profile that may contribute to increased systemic inflammation. Taken together, these data strongly suggest that obesity may trigger an unbalanced systemic and local inflammatory response that results in cognitive dysfunction. Unfortunately, targeting inflammatory processes via global pharmacological strategies such as ketoprofen should not be proposed for all patients because of important side effects (e.g., nephrotoxicity), and those treatments should be monitored closely in terms of dosage and duration to adapt to each patient [].

The mechanism by which obesity contributes to such inflammatory responses is not clear. First, obesity is currently associated with a defect in metabolic homeostasis, and several studies have demonstrated the deleterious effects of diabetes and metabolic syndrome in human [, ] and rodent [] cohorts subjected to different types of surgery. Even if no modification of the metabolic phenotype has been observed after tibial fracture, we cannot rule out a potential role of obesity-associated chronic metabolic disturbance in the onset of obesity-related PND. However, a preliminary study promoting the onset of nonobese diabetes in mice via a high-fat/high-sugar diet demonstrated that metabolic alterations alone are not sufficient to promote tibial fracture-induced local hyperinflammation (data not shown). Consequently, we focused our attention on a better understanding of the role of white adipose tissue during obesity in PND development, hypothesizing that white adipose tissue could act through cellular transfer, secretion or innervation. Interestingly, we observed that subcutaneous adipose tissue in obese mice, which is specifically localized close to the site of surgery, is involved in an increase in inflammation. Indeed, even though surgery did not impact adipose tissue weight or adipocyte size distribution, immune cells and adipogenic markers were altered in the subcutaneous adipose tissue localized close to the fractured site in both ND- and HFD-fed mice without a change in the other white adipose tissue depots (i.e., the visceral and contralateral subcutaneous adipose tissues). This result, together with the observed hyperinflammation and the large numbers of proinflammatory immune cells in the white adipose tissue of obese mice in the basal state, reinforces the concept that locally altered white adipose tissue could mediate surgery-induced cognitive disorders. We definitively validated this notion by ablating the whole local subcutaneous adipose tissue in obese mice and showing protection from PND. This result paves the way for a new understanding of PND, as it highlights the inflammatory state of the local adipose tissue rather than the systemic profile that contributes to the condition. However, to reinforce the translational potential of our results, our findings here must be generalized to other models of invasive surgery. Indeed, we assume that sternotomy-associated surgery, which is often practiced in patients with obesity for cardiac issues, preferentially impacts visceral adipose tissue. Consequently, evaluating the extent to which the well-known proinflammatory profile of obese visceral adipose tissue may locally contribute to major cognitive decline and/or longer PND is highly important. In line with these findings, in a preliminary study, we observed that laparotomy induced a decrease in BDNF and tight junction protein (Claudin5/Occludin) expression in the brains of HFD-fed mice compared with those of ND-fed controls (data not shown). Further experiments are needed to better understand the role of the differently localized fat pads in terms of the type of surgery. Another limitation of our study resides in the generalizability of the obtained results to both sexes. Although clinical results do not differ between males and females, it will be of great interest to study the consequences of both obesity and surgery in female mouse models to better assess the potential protective effects of estrogens. For example, estradiol supplementation protected old female mice from laparotomy-induced PND [], whereas in humans, no association was found between estradiol supplementation and improved cognition after cardiac surgery []. Another study demonstrated that estrogen supplementation prevents PND in laparotomy-induced cognitive decline in aged male mice []. Moreover, while LPS injection induced cognitive decline and microglia activation in aged male rats, this was not observed in aged females or in aged ovariectomized females, demonstrating the sexual dimorphism in the response may exist independently of ovarian hormones []. Thus, no clear conclusions can yet be drawn regarding the mechanisms underlying potential sexual dimorphism in PND, and future studies will need to address this limitation. Finally, to envision new preventive strategies for patients with obesity who will undergo invasive surgery, we showed that obese mice under calorie restriction do not present surgery-associated cognitive dysfunction. This result is reinforced by basal cognitive improvement in humans who exhibit a loss of adiposity two years after bariatric surgery []. Taken together, these data suggest that achieving significant weight loss prior to surgery may be an effective strategy to prevent obesity-associated PND. However, several important considerations must be taken into account when translating these findings to the clinic. Indeed, precautions are needed regarding the risk of malnutrition in patients with obesity []. Patients with obesity who undergo calorie restriction may suffer from malnutrition due to deficiencies in protein micronutrients, which can have a negative impact on their morbidity/mortality. Moreover, drastic weight loss aggravates the impact of malnutrition on patient health, cognitive status, psychology and physical status, increasing the risk of sarcopenia []. Thus, the feasibility of preoperative weight loss in obese surgical patients depends on the timing of surgery and the patient’s ability to adhere to caloric restriction. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of preoperative weight loss interventions in gastrointestinal cancer surgery found that intentional preoperative weight loss was feasible, with completion rates ≥ 96.9%, while preserving skeletal muscle mass and nutritional parameters []. Longer preoperative waiting periods, combined with structured dietary programs and close monitoring, may further improve the feasibility of weight loss interventions. Moreover, for emergency surgeries, anti-inflammatory strategies, such as preoperative dietary interventions rich in omega-3 fatty acids or targeted anti-inflammatory agents, represent complementary approaches that may also reduce PND risk, although their efficacy and safety in this population remain to be established. Clinical trials investigating the modulation of inflammatory response in bariatric surgery are currently ongoing to evaluate how different strategies affect inflammation after surgery ( NCT06915558 ). Finally, future clinical trials should test whether preoperative weight loss and anti-inflammatory strategies are effective and safe in obese surgical patients. These trials should compare preoperative calorie restriction with or without micronutrient and anti-inflammatory nutritional support, versus standard care. Primary outcomes should include cognitive function at several time points, morbidity and mortality, sarcopenia, and nutritional status. Adding inflammatory biomarkers and brain imaging could help clarify the mechanisms and identify which patients are most likely to benefit.
