sections.methods:
All animal experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Capital Medical University. Animals were housed in cages under controlled environmental conditions, with temperatures maintained between 22°C and 24°C, humidity at 40%–70%, and 12-h light/12-h dark cycle. BK channel knockout (BK-KO) rats were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 approaches as previously described (). All rats used in this study were male and were sacrificed after fasting or feeding for 24 h, unless stated otherwise. All experiments were performed in 12- to 16-week-old rats.

All mice used in all experiments were on a C57BL/6J background and were male. All animal experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Capital Medical University. All mice used in this study were bred and housed under specific pathogen-free conditions (12 h/12 h light and dark cycle, 22°C ± 2°C). BK flox/flox mice (Cyagen Biosciences) and Adipoq-Cre mice (Cyagen Biosciences, China) were generated through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. BK adipocyte-specific knockout (BK adipo−/− ) mice were generated by mating the floxed-BK mouse strain with adipoq-Cre transgenic mice, to obtain adipoq-Cre +/− BK flox/flox mice. Adipoq-Cre −/− BK flox/flox mice (BK adipo+/+ ) littermates were used as controls. Age- and sex-matched mice were co-housed and used for all the experiments in this study. Genotyping was carried out using tail tips that were incubated with 200 μl 50 M NaoH buffer for 30 min at 100°C. And we add 16 μl 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) to the buffer. Genotyping was performed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using Cre-, LoxP1-, and LoxP2-specific primers. BK adipo−/− mice displayed a 200 bp band for Cre, a 239 bp band for LoxP1, and a 279 bp band for LoxP2. BK adipo+/+ mice showed no band for Cre, but identical band sizes for LoxP1 and LoxP2. The primers for mice genotyping are listed in .

Rats (or mice) were individually housed in metabolic cages (maintained at 22 ± 2°C, 40%–70% humidity, with a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle) for a 24-h acclimation period with ad libitum access to food and water to minimize stress-induced disturbances in feeding and drinking behaviors. After acclimation, the metabolic cages were cleaned, and the animals were returned to the cages. A fixed amount of feed (50 g per cage) and autoclaved distilled water (100 g per cage) were provided, followed by continuous monitoring for 5 days. Daily food intake was calculated as "initial feed weight minus remaining feed weight," and daily water intake was calculated as "initial water weight minus remaining water weight." The average daily food intake and water intake per animal (rat or mouse) was determined by averaging the measurements over the 5-day period.

12-week-old male SD rats were randomly assigned to either the ad libitum feeding group or the 24 h fasting group on a per-cage basis. For the fasting model, all cage bedding was replaced with fresh bedding prior to the start of the experiment. Rats in the fasting group were subjected to complete food deprivation for 24 h but were provided with ad libitum access to water throughout the fasting period. Control rats in the ad libitum group were given free access to fresh food and water under the same housing conditions.

12-week-old BK KO and WT rats were fasted for 24 h or fasted for 24 h and then re-fed ad libitum for 6 h.

6-week-old male BK adipo−/− and BK adipo+/+ mice were randomly assigned to two groups and fed ad libitum for 16 weeks: one group received a chow diet (CD) (LabDiet 5001, USA), a nutritionally complete maintenance diet with 10% of calories from fat; the other group was given a high-fat diet (HFD) containing 60% of calories from fat (Research Diets). Weight gain in the mice was assessed biweekly over the course of the study.

For glucose tolerance tests (GTT), mice were overnight fasted for 14 h with free access to water. Following the fasting period, baseline blood glucose levels were measured from tail vein blood samples using a handheld glucometer. Mice were then administered an intraperitoneal injection of glucose (1 g/kg body weight). Blood glucose concentrations were subsequently measured at 15, 30, 60, and 120 min post-injection. Glucose levels were recorded for subsequent analysis.

For insulin tolerance tests (ITT), mice were fasted for 4 h with ad libitum access to water. Following the fasting period, baseline blood glucose levels were measured from tail vein blood samples using a handheld glucometer. Mice were then administered an intraperitoneal injection of insulin (0.75 U/kg body weight). Blood glucose concentrations were subsequently measured at 15, 30, 60, and 120 min post-injection. Glucose levels were recorded for subsequent analysis.

Body composition was assessed in 12-week-old rats using the EchoMRI-900™ small animal in vivo body composition analyzer (Echo Medical Systems). Total fat mass and lean mass were quantified by Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and the ratios of fat mass and lean mass to total body weight were calculated.

For precise quantification of total fat mass and lean mass in mice, animals were anesthetized with 1.5% isoflurane in O 2 and positioned within a small animal body composition analysis and imaging system (small animal PET/CT/SPECT three-in-one system) for detailed analysis.

In this study, lean body mass was defined as body components excluding fat and free water, mainly comprising bone, skeletal muscle, and visceral tissues. Fat mass was defined as the total fat tissue. It should be noted that lean body mass is not equal to total body mass minus fat mass.

For metabolic cage analysis, mice were housed in the Pan Lab/Harvard Apparatus metabolic cage system at week 16 of HFD or CD feeding, with one mouse per chamber. The mice were allowed to adapt to the metabolic cages for 12 h, and then the oxygen consumption rate (VO 2 ), carbon dioxide production rate (VCO 2 ), and energy expenditure (EE) were measured continuously for 48 h. Metabolic cages were maintained at 22 ± 2°C with 40%–70% humidity and a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle.

Following body composition assessment, mice were euthanized, and various adipose tissue depots were carefully dissected. The iWAT, eWAT, and BAT were excised, weighed to determine individual fat pad mass, and processed for subsequent analyses. Tissue samples were either fixed in 10% formalin solution for histological examination or snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C for further investigations.

Upon dissection, adipose tissue samples were immediately fixed in 10% formalin solution in 0.1 M PBS overnight, then embedded in paraffin. Paraffin sections were cut at a thickness of 5 μm and mounted onto glass slides. For morphological analysis, sections were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and stained with H&E according to established protocols. Stained sections were dehydrated, cleared, and mounted with coverslips. Digital images were acquired utilizing a Zeiss light microscope. To evaluate adipocyte area within the specified adipose tissue sections, ImageJ software was employed. For each sample, approximately 20–50 adipocytes from at least three randomly selected fields were analyzed to ensure representative sampling.

Upon completion of the dietary intervention, blood samples were collected from mice after a 12 h overnight fast. Serum was separated by centrifugation at 3,000 rpm for 15 min at 4°C, and aliquots were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C until further analysis. Serum concentrations of various metabolic parameters were determined using specific kits as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Free fatty acid (FFA) levels were measured using NEFA-HR reagents (Wako Chemicals). Glycerol concentrations were measured using free glycerol reagents (Cat# F6428, Sigma-Aldrich). The levels of total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) were measured using kits from Beijing Sino Bio-Tech Research Institute (Beijing, China).

Adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) were extracted from the epididymal fat pads of 3-month-old male SD rats using our laboratory's established method (). The fat pads were minced and digested in 5 ml of Krebs-Ringer solution (Cat# K4002, Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 0.8 mg/ml type I collagenase (Cat# LS004196 , Worthington), 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.4), and 1% free fatty acid-free bovine serum albumin (Cat# V900933, Sigma-Aldrich). Following a 50-min digestion at 37°C in an air bath with agitation at 100 cycles/minute, the cells were sieved through 80# and then 400# steel mesh before being centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 10 min. ADSCs were cultured in a 6-well plate using DMEM/F12 (1:1 vol/vol) medium (Cat# 10-092-CV, Corning) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Cat# 10100-147, Gibco), 100 U/ml penicillin, and 0.1 mg/ml streptomycin (Cat# 15140122, Gibco). The cells were maintained in a humidified cell incubator with 5% CO 2 at 37°C.

Upon reaching 85%–95% confluence, the cells were exposed to differentiation medium I, comprising 5 μg/ml insulin (Cat# P3376-400IU, Beyotime), 0.5 mM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (Cat# I5879, Sigma-Aldrich), 1 μM dexamethasone (Cat# D4902, Sigma-Aldrich), 5 μM troglitazone (Cat# HY-50935, MCE), and 10% FBS in DMEM/F12 (1:1 vol/vol). After 48 h, differentiation medium I was replaced with differentiation medium II, containing 5 μg/ml insulin, 5 μM troglitazone, and 10% FBS in DMEM/F12 (1:1 vol/vol), with cells incubated for an additional 48 h. Subsequently, cells were cultured in DMEM/F12 (1:1 vol/vol) supplemented with 10% FBS for 4 days, with the medium refreshed every alternate day. Following the induction of differentiation, the necessary experiments were carried out.

Glycerol content released in culture medium of adipocytes served as an index of lipolysis. Differentiated mature adipocytes were washed twice with PBS to remove residual medium, then incubated in phenol red-free, serum-free DMEM/F12 medium supplemented with 1% fatty acid-free BSA. Cells were stimulated with either 1 μM CL-316243 (Cat# C5976, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM Forskolin (Cat# HY-15371, MCE), or 1 mM 8-Bromo-cAMP (Cat# HY-12306A, MCE) for 1 h at 37°C in an incubator with 5% CO 2 . Control cells were incubated under identical conditions without stimulation. Following incubation, conditioned medium was then collected and determined by absorbance at 490 nm, by use of a glycerol assay kit from Applygen (China). The lipolysis data were normalized to each milligram of protein by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) quantification.

ADSCs were seeded in glass-bottom culture dishes and differentiated into mature adipocytes following the aforementioned protocol. On day 8, the adipocytes were washed three times with Hank's Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS) and subsequently loaded with 5 μM Fluo-4 AM by incubation at 37°C for 30 min. Fluorescence imaging was performed using a TCS SP8 STED confocal microscope (Leica) with an excitation wavelength set at 488 nm. The acquired fluorescence signals were quantified for intensity using ImageJ software, and further image analysis was conducted according to previously established methods ().

Adipose tissues underwent homogenization, and adipose cells were lysed using a standard RIPA buffer supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Cat# 11206893001, Roche) and a phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Cat# P5726, Sigma-Aldrich) on ice for 40 min. The lysates were subsequently centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4°C to remove insoluble debris. Total protein concentration was quantified using the BCA method. Following this, equal amounts of protein (20 μg per group) were separated via 4%–20% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore). Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk in Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) at room temperature for 1 h, then incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies. After washing three times with TBST, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using a standard electrochemiluminescence (ECL) kit (Cat# KGP1123, KeyGEN BioTECH) and imaged with a chemiluminescence imaging system. Band densities were quantified using ImageJ software. The primary antibodies utilized included p-HSL (Ser660) (Cat #45804, Cell Signaling), p-HSL (Ser565) (Cat #4137, Cell Signaling), HSL (Cat #4107, Cell Signaling), ATGL (Cat #2138, Cell Signaling), Phospho-PKA substrate (RRXS∗/T∗) (Cat #9624, Cell Signaling), p-AKT (Ser473) (Cat #9018, Cell Signaling), and AKT (Cat #2920, Cell Signaling). HSP90 (Cat #A5027, ABclonal) and β-Actin (Cat #66009-1-Ig, Proteintech) densities were employed as internal controls for total protein levels.

Total RNA was isolated from tissues and cells utilizing the RNeasy kit (Cat# RC112-01, Vazyme) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. RNA concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Subsequently, the total RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA employing the FastKing RT Kit (Cat# KR116, Tiangen) following the manufacturer's protocol. For the quantification of mRNA expression, qRT-PCR was conducted using the 2X PowerUp™ SYBR™ Green Master Mix (Cat# A25742, Applied Biosystems). The expression levels of individual genes were normalized to the expression of 36B4 or β-Actin using the ΔΔCt method. All reactions were performed in triplicate. The primer sequences utilized are detailed in .

RNA-seq assay was conducted on primary cultured adipocytes isolated from the epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) of BK KO and WT rats, following the methods previously described (). In simple terms, total RNA was extracted using an RNAprep Pure Tissue Kit (Cat# DP431, Tiangen) in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. The construction of the transcriptome library, sequencing, and data analysis were carried out by OE Biotech Co, Ltd (Shanghai, China) and Novogene Co, Ltd (Beijing, China). Firstly, the research data set from the laboratory was normalized and standardized. The R package "limma" (version 3.56.2) was utilized to analyze the data from five WT samples and five KO samples, with the conditions for differential gene selection set at P value < 0.05 and |Log2FC| > 1. The differential genes were visualized using volcano plots and heatmaps created with the R packages "ggplot2" (version 3.5.1) and "heatmap" (version 1.0.12). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted on the selected differentially expressed genes, employing the species annotation "org.Rn.e.g.db", while Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis utilized "Rno" as the species annotation. A P value of < 0.05, sorted in ascending order, was used as the selection criterion to identify the top 10 KEGG pathways as well as the GO biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions. The results of the GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were then visualized.

RNA extracted from eWAT of BK KO rats (n = 4) and their corresponding littermates (n = 4) was utilized for analysis. Total RNA isolation was carried out using the RNeasy kit (Cat# RC112-01, Vazyme) following the recommended protocols. Post-extraction, RNA quality was assessed using the Agilent Technologies 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technology, USA) and agarose gel electrophoresis. Qualified RNA were quantified using the Qubit3.0 with the QubitTM RNA Broad Range Assay kit (Cat# Q10210 , ThermoFisher). For RNA-seq investigations, stranded RNA sequencing libraries were generated with the KC-Digital™ Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit utilizing 2 μg of total RNA. Library fragments spanning 200–500 bp were enriched, and sequencing was conducted on the Novaseq 6000 sequencer (Illumina) using the PE150 model. Initial raw data underwent filtration with Trimmomatic (version 0.36) to remove low-quality reads and adaptor sequence contaminants. Clean reads were further processed with custom scripts to address duplication bias introduced during library preparation and sequencing.

Differential gene expression analysis between groups was performed using the edgeR package (version 3.12.1), excluding genes with zero read counts. Statistical significance in gene expression alterations was determined by a P value of < 0.05 and fold-change values exceeding 2. Subsequent gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted for all genes identified using GSEA software. Gene sets were considered to be significantly enriched with a P value of < 0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.25.

All experiments necessitating statistical analysis were conducted a minimum of three times, yielding consistent outcomes. All data were verified for normal distribution using the Shapiro-Wilk test before statistical analysis, and P > 0.05 was considered indicative of data conforming to a normal distribution. For normally distributed data, unpaired two-tailed Student's t test was employed for comparisons between two groups. Comparisons involving multiple groups were assessed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test or two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s post hoc analysis for continuous variables. For non-normally distributed data, Mann–Whitney U test (two-group comparisons) and Kruskal-Wallis H test followed by Dunn’s post hoc test (multiple-group comparisons) were employed. Data were shown as mean ± SEM. A significance level of P < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant for all tests.
sections.results:
To demonstrate the role of BK channels in adipose tissue, we constructed homozygous BK knockout (BK-KO) rats (BK −/− ) (). Weekly monitoring of rat body weights, ranging from 4 to 12 weeks, revealed that BK-KO rats exhibited significantly lower weight gain compared to WT rats (A, B). Metabolic cage assays evaluating 24-h food and water intake in 12-week-old WT and BK-KO rats demonstrated no notable differences (C, D), indicating that the difference in body weight was not related to food intake. Subsequent EchoMRI scans and adipose tissue analyses confirmed a marked reduction in fat mass, which contributed to the diminished body weight observed in BK-KO rats (E, F). Notably, BK-KO rats exhibited a higher proportion of lean mass to body weight, a significantly lower ratio of fat mass to body weight, and a reduced fat-to-lean mass ratio in comparison to WT rats (G-I). Furthermore, the adipose tissues in different parts of the body showed a significant reduction in inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) and visceral epididymal adipose tissue (eWAT) in BK-KO rats, and the ratio of WAT mass to body weight was significantly reduced, with eWAT exhibiting the most significant reduction in ratio. Conversely, there were no substantial changes observed in the scapular region brown adipose tissue (BAT) (J-L). Together, these results underscore that systemic BK channel knockout leads to a substantial decrease in WAT mass, accounting for the body weight loss. The mechanisms underlying the pronounced reduction in eWAT and associated factors will be further investigated.

To investigate the reasons and related mechanisms for the significant reduction of eWAT mass when BK channels were knockout, transcriptomics based on an RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) assay was used to investigate the differences in gene expression between primary adipocytes derived from the eWAT of BK-KO and WT rats. We conducted a reanalysis of the previous RNA-seq results obtained by our research group (). We conducted standardization of the dataset to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (A). According to the defined criteria, a total of 357 DEGs were screened out in the BK-KO group in comparison with the WT group, of which 198 genes were upregulated and 159 genes were downregulated (B). There were significant differences in the overall gene composition through cluster analysis (C). To identify the biological functions and signaling pathways related to lipid metabolism, DEGs were used for gene ontology biological process (GO-BP) enrichment and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that the enrichment of DEGs was associated with lipolysis-related pathways, namely PI 3 K-AKT signaling pathway, cAMP signaling pathway and AMPK signaling pathway in adipocytes (D). Subsequently, the DEGs enrichment in the GO biological terms performing functions in biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and molecular function (MF), we found that BK-KO is closely related to glycerolipid metabolic process in BP enrichment analysis (E). RNA-seq results indicate that deletion of the BK channels might promote the lipolysis process through the cAMP, PI 3 K-AKT and/or AMPK signaling pathway.

Subsequently, we employed transcriptomics based on RNA-seq assays to investigate the differences in gene expression between the eWAT of BK-KO and WT rats. As illustrated in the volcanic plot (A), a total of 342 DEGs—comprising 174 upregulated genes and 168 downregulated genes—were identified between the eWAT samples isolated from the BK-KO and WT rats. This identification was based on the criteria of adjusted P value < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1. Furthermore, DEGs were presented in a heatmap (B), clearly indicating significant differences in gene expression profiles between the two groups. To gain further biological insights regarding DEGs, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed. The results indicated that two pathways closely related to lipid metabolism were significantly upregulated, namely, the metabolic pathway and cAMP signaling pathway (C). The RNA-seq results are validated by the primary adipocyte RNA-seq results, indicating that the deficiency of BK channels could regulate the lipolysis process.

To clarify whether BK channels in adipocytes affect lipolysis, we fasted WT and BK-KO rats for 24 h. When subjected to 24 h of fasting, BK-KO rats showed a greater decrease in the ratio of the body weight change to total body weight after fasting than WT rats (A, B). The findings indicated that the magnitude of weight reduction observed in BK-KO rats is substantially higher compared to that in WT rats. We also measured the weights of different adipose tissues in the fed state and after 24 h of fasting. The results showed that under fasting conditions, the adipose tissue weight of BK-KO rats was significantly reduced, and the ratio of adipose tissue weight to body weight was also significantly decreased, with eWAT being particularly affected (C–H), which may be an important reason for the observed body weight loss. Within the same genotype, compared to the fed state, after 24 h of fasting, there was no statistically significant reduction in the weight of iWAT and eWAT adipose stores or the percentage of adipose store weight relative to body weight in WT and BK-KO rats; only a downward trend was observed (C–H). This finding may be related to the short duration of fasting, as 24 h of fasting has a limited effect on mobilizing fat reserves, not reaching a level detectable by gross weight measurement. Hemoglobin and eosin (H&E) staining and adipocyte size analysis of eWAT revealed smaller adipocytes in BK-KO rats than in WT rats, under both fed and fasting conditions (I–K). Direct comparison of adipocyte size within the same genotype between fed and fasting states showed that after 24 h of fasting, the adipocyte area of both WT and BK-KO rats was significantly reduced, and the cell diameter was correspondingly shortened (J, K), indicating that 24 h of fasting is sufficient to induce significant changes in adipocyte morphology, demonstrating that lipolytic mobilization has been initiated.

It is widely recognized that the functions of ATGL and HSL, pivotal lipases for fat mobilization, hold significant importance in adipose tissue (). The RNA-Seq analysis suggested that BK channels affect the lipolysis process through the cAMP pathway. Consequently, we used western blotting to determine the effects of the BK channel deficiency on the expression levels of various proteins associated with lipolysis in vivo. Our results demonstrated that consistent with a reduction in eWAT mass (D, G), the BK channel deficiency significantly increased the phosphorylation level of HSL on Ser660, which indicates the activation of HSL (L, M). Meanwhile, ATGL protein expression levels were significantly elevated after the BK channel deficiency. Notably, however, the phosphorylation level of HSL on Ser565 was not altered (L, M), which is recognized as a negative regulatory element (, , ). The abovementioned data tentatively suggest that BK channel deficiency accelerates lipolysis of eWAT after 24 h of fasting.

To prevent the impact of BK channel deficiency in non-adipose tissues on adipose tissue lipolysis, we subsequently constructed adipocyte-specific BK knockout mice (BK adipo−/− ) using Crisp/Cas9 technology (A). Adipoq-Cre −/− BK flox/flox littermate mice (BK adipo+/+ ) were used as wild-type controls. Genotyping was verified by agarose gel electrophoresis, and qRT-PCR confirmed the effective and specific knockout of BK channels in adipose tissue (B, C).

After feeding 6-week-old BK adipo−/− mice and their BK adipo+/+ controls with a 60% high-fat diet (HFD) for 16 weeks, significant observations emerged. BK adipo−/− mice displayed significantly lower weight gain compared to HFD-fed BK adipo+/+ mice (A–D). Subsequent EchoMRI scans and adipose tissue analysis affirmed that the reduced body weight in BK adipo−/− mice stemmed from decreased fat mass relative to BK adipo+/+ mice, with no notable changes in lean tissue weight (A–E). Photographic comparison of different adipose tissues from BK adipo−/− mice and BK adipo+/+ mice demonstrated a notable reduction in WAT in BK adipo−/− mice (F). Notably, the reduced weight gain in HFD-fed BK adipo−/− mice was not associated with variations in food and water intake compared to HFD-fed BK adipo+/+ mice (G, H). We examined blood parameters associated with obesity, including total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and low-density lipoprotein (LDL). The results showed that these parameters were improved in BK adipo−/− mice (I–L).

BK adipo−/− mice had greater glucose and insulin tolerances compared to BK adipo+/+ mice (M–P). In conclusion, adipocyte-specific deletion of BK channels protected mice from HFD-induced obesity and insulin resistance. Meantime we fed 6-week-old BK adipo−/− mice and their BK adipo+/+ control mice a normal chow diet (CD) for 16 weeks. The majority of the phenotypes observed in BK adipo−/− mice on the HFD regimen diminished when comparing BK adipo−/− mice with BK adipo+/+ mice under the CD diet condition (A–T).

In alignment with our fasting trials, histological analyses through H&E staining of eWAT revealed a reduction in the size of adipocytes in BK adipo−/− mice compared to BK adipo+/+ mice under HFD conditions (E–G). Consistent with our fasting experiment results, under HFD conditions, compared with BK adipo+/+ mice, BK adipo−/− mice exhibited significantly increased phosphorylation of HSL at Ser660 in eWAT, while phosphorylation of HSL at Ser565 remained unchanged. In contrast to the eWAT findings in BK-KO rats, the expression levels of ATGL remained unaltered in BK adipo−/− mice (H, I). After 16 weeks of HFD feeding, there was a noticeable trend towards increased release of glycerol and free fatty acid (FFA) into circulation in BK adipo−/− mice (J, K). This indicates that BK adipo−/− mice are resistant to HFD-induced weight gain, at least in part due to stimulated lipolysis. We further performed indirect calorimetry analysis and found that HFD-fed BK adipo−/− mice exhibited significantly elevated oxygen consumption rate (VO 2 ), carbon dioxide production rate (VCO 2 ), and energy expenditure (EE) compared to their BK adipo+/+ littermate controls. Following ANCOVA adjustment with lean mass as the covariate, statistically significant differences were observed for VO 2 ( P = 0.0291), VCO 2 ( P = 0.0454), and EE ( P = 0.0319) (Q–S). Similar experimental assessments were conducted on CD-fed BK adipo−/− mice and their BK adipo+/+ counterparts, revealing no discernible difference between the two groups (A–J), indicating that the effect is specifically triggered by metabolic stress. Taken together, these results demonstrate that adipocyte-specific deletion of BK channels reduces fat mass through concurrent enhancement of lipolysis and energy expenditure.

To eliminate potential confounding effects from other cells in adipose tissue, epididymal adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) obtained from BK-KO and WT rats were induced into adipocytes and subsequently subjected to further investigations (A). The β 3 receptor agonist CL-316243 was used to induce lipolysis in adipocytes. Results indicated a significant increase in glycerol levels in the culture medium of BK channel deficiency adipocytes 1 h after CL-316243 stimulation (B). For a brief (1-h) intervention on BK channel function in mature adipocytes in the presence of CL-316243, a BK channel antagonist, PAX (3 μM), and a BK channel agonist, NS1619 (20 μM), were utilized. It was observed that inhibition of BK channels significantly increased glycerol levels in the culture medium in the presence of CL-316243. Whereas BK channel activation reduced glycerol levels in the culture medium under the same conditions (C).

To gain insight into the related mechanisms through which BK channel deficiency accelerates lipolysis, we examined the levels and phosphorylation status of key proteins regulating lipolysis in adipocytes in vitro. Following CL-316243 stimulation for 1 h, the phosphorylation levels of HSL at Ser660 were significantly elevated in the context of BK channel deficiency (D, E). Moreover, the mRNA levels of HSL and ATGL were significantly elevated in BK channel-deficient adipocytes (F). Using the BK channel antagonist PAX (3 μM) and the BK channel agonist NS1619 (20 μM) for a short (1 h) intervention on the BK channel function in mature adipocytes in the presence of CL-316243, we found that inhibition of the BK channels significantly increased phosphorylation levels of HSL at Ser660 in the presence of CL-316243. This effect diminished upon BK channel activation (G, H). Interestingly, there were no significant changes in the mRNA expression levels of HSL and ATGL when BK channel function was either inhibited or activated (I).

Taken together, these results support that BK channels deficiency or inhibition enhances CL-316243-stimulated lipolysis in mature adipocytes in vitro. Meanwhile, activation of BK channels suppresses lipolytic response to CL-316243-stimulation.

It has been established that the phosphorylation level of HSL at the Ser660 site is regulated by PKA. Following a 24-h fasting period, we noted that the phosphorylation level of the PKA substrate in BK-KO eWAT was significantly higher in comparison to WT eWAT (A, B). This finding also corroborates the RNA-seq analysis, which indicates that the absence of BK channels promotes lipolysis through the cAMP/PKA/HSL signaling pathway. To further elucidate the role of BK channels in regulating lipolysis through cAMP/PKA/HSL pathway, we pretreated mature adipocytes derived from BK-KO and WT rats for 1 h using H89 (10 μM), an inhibitor of PKA, a key protein in lipolysis, while simultaneously administering CL-316243 to stimulate lipolysis. Our findings revealed that BK channel deficiency led to increased glycerol levels in the culture medium during CL-316243-stimulated lipolysis compared to the WT group. However, the effect of BK-KO on increased glycerol release disappeared after treatment with H89 (C). In addition, the BK-KO-induced upregulation of HSL-Ser660 phosphorylation was eliminated after inhibition of PKA by H89 (D, E). The absence of BK channels promotes the release of glycerol from the culture medium and enhances phosphorylation levels of HSL at Ser660 in the presence of CL-316243, which can be mimicked by the adenylate cyclase activator forskolin (10 μM) or 8-bromo-cAMP (1 mM), a soluble cAMP analog (F–H). These results collectively indicate that BK-KO promotes the lipolysis process by activating the cAMP/PKA/HSL pathway.

It is well-known that the activity of BK channels, as calcium (Ca 2+ )-activated potassium (K + ) channels, is closely related to changes in intracellular Ca 2+ concentration (, ). Previous studies have demonstrated that sustained elevation of intracellular calcium primarily promotes lipid synthesis, whereas the activation of lipolysis depends more critically on transient, localized Ca 2+ spikes (, ). To further investigate the role of Ca 2+ signaling in BK channel deficiency-induced lipolysis, we examined intracellular Ca 2+ dynamics in mature adipocytes differentiated in vitro from BK-KO and WT rats following stimulation with CL-316243. Our results showed that, compared to WT adipocytes, both BK-KO adipocytes and WT adipocytes pre-incubated with PAX to inhibit BK channel function exhibited transient increases in both the average and Δfold change in fluorescence intensity of fluo-4 (I, J). These data indicate that under β3-adrenergic stimulation, genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of BK channels transiently elevates intracellular Ca 2+ levels, thereby modulating the cAMP/PKA/HSL signaling axis to promote lipolysis.

Our previous results showed that phosphorylation levels of AKT-Ser473 were elevated by insulin stimulation, and the inhibition of BK channels hindered this process (). Meanwhile, it has been reported that elevated phosphorylation levels of AKT-Ser473 can inhibit cAMP levels and thus indirectly inhibit the lipolysis process (). After 24 h of fasting, there was no significant difference in the phosphorylation levels of AKT-Ser473 between WT eWAT and BK-KO eWAT. Moreover, in both the WT and BK-KO groups, there was no statistically significant difference in the p-AKT (Ser473)/AKT ratio between the fed and fasted states (A, B). Meanwhile, inhibiting BK channel function in the presence of CL-316243 did not impact the phosphorylation levels of AKT-Ser473 (C, D), but it resulted in elevated phosphorylation of HSL-Ser660 and enhanced lipolysis (G, H). These combined results indicate that the inhibition of BK channel function involves a signaling pathway independent of the PI3K-AKT signaling axis, which can directly regulate the lipolysis process.
sections.discussion:
The relationship between adipocyte lipolysis and energy homeostasis is crucial, as any dysregulation in adipocyte lipolytic mechanisms can disrupt homeostasis and contribute to metabolic disorders (, , ). Excessive lipolysis in WAT can lead to systemic insulin resistance and play a role in the development of diabetes (). It is essential to delve deeper into the finely tuned regulatory mechanisms of lipolysis to identify new targets that can modulate the rate of lipolysis, offering resistance to obesity while preventing lipotoxicity-induced diabetes resulting from excessive lipolysis. Fasting is not only a means of dietary restriction, but also a strategy for metabolic regulation, making it a topic of great interest to those seeking a deeper understanding of the processes associated with lipolysis. During periods of energy deprivation, triacylglycerols stored in WAT are hydrolyzed by lipolytic enzymes, releasing fatty acids (FA) into the circulation for utilization by other organs as an energy source. This study has demonstrated that BK channels exert an inhibitory effect on PKA activation-induced lipolysis in adipocytes. It is known that BK expression in adipocytes is influenced by nutritional status, and increased BK channel expression is observed in the adipose tissue of obese individuals (). The study findings indicate that BK channel deficiency or pharmacological inhibition accelerates lipolysis, whereas pharmacological activation inhibits this process. Specifically, enhanced activation of HSL was observed in BK-KO rats and BK adipo−/− mice. BK adipo−/− mice displayed resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and improved insulin sensitivity.

In our study, we initially observed decreased body weight and reduced WAT mass in BK-KO rats compared to WT controls, with visceral WAT exhibiting the most significant reduction ().Consistent with previous findings different fat depots showed different phenotypes responses to fasting, and visceral WAT was particularly sensitive to lipolytic stimulation (, , ). To further explore the underlying mechanisms for the significant reduction in eWAT weight following BK deletion, we performed RNA-Seq analysis. Enrichment analysis of DEGs revealed pathways associated with the cAMP and PI 3 K-AKT pathway linked to lipolytic metabolism (). As a critical intracellular second messenger, cAMP responds to various hormonal stimuli such as adrenaline and glucagon. These hormones act through G protein-coupled receptors on the cell surface, activating adenylate cyclase (AC) and subsequently increasing intracellular cAMP levels. Previous studies have shown that cAMP promotes lipolysis by activating its downstream-effector, PKA (). Based on these observations, we propose that BK channel deficiency influences lipid metabolism via β 3 -adrenergic-mediated PKA activation, leading to enhanced expression and activation of key lipolytic enzymes. Under fasting conditions, our results showed that BK channel knockout led to increased protein expression of ATGL, increased phosphorylation of HSL at the Ser660 site (), and upregulated levels of PKA substrate phosphorylation (). Moreover, in vitro experiments revealed that stimulation with CL-316243, forskolin and the 8-bromo-cAMP significantly enhanced lipolysis in BK-deficient adipocytes ( and ), whereas pharmacological inhibition of PKA with H89 completely abolished this effect (). Collectively, these findings indicate that BK- channel deficiency promotes lipolysis by activating the cAMP/PKA/HSL pathway.

Research by Illison et al. has indicated that BK channel deficiency protects mice from HFD-induced weight gain and fat accumulation, with adipocytes relying on UCP1 -mediated energy dissipation to reduce lipid storage (). It has also been established that the induction of lipolysis is essential for UCP1-dependent energy dissipation in adipocytes (, ). To delve deeper into this phenomenon, we constructed BK adipo−/− mice and subjected them to via HFD-induced obesity. Consistent with the findings of Illison et al. , we observed resistance to HFD-induced obesity in our BK adipo−/− mouse model. Importantly, our study extends these observations by providing the first evidence that BK adipo−/− mice display a significant increase in HSL phosphorylation at the Ser660 site, thereby promoting lipolysis (). In contrast, under a CD, BK adipo−/− mice did not exhibit elevated HSL phosphorylation at the Ser660 site (), indicating that the effect is specifically triggered by metabolic stress. These results suggest that BK channel deletion heightens adipocyte sensitivity to β 3 -adrenergic-stimulated lipolysis, leading to a rapid reduction of visceral fat mass and resistance to HFD-induced obesity. Notably, our study reveals a previously unrecognized role for BK channels in regulating lipolytic processes through the modulation of HSL phosphorylation. Furthermore, growing evidence suggests that chronically elevated FFA levels can promote lipid accumulation and insulin resistance in non-adipose tissues (, , ). The markedly improved insulin sensitivity observed in BK adipo−/− mice raises the possibility that additional mechanisms may also contribute to this phenotype. Indeed, compared to BK adipo+/+ littermates, BK adipo−/− mice exhibited not only increased eWAT lipolysis but also elevated energy expenditure (), which may further explain their leaner phenotype—thereby extending and refining the observations originally reported by Illisonet et al. In conclusion, our findings establish BK channels as negative regulators of β 3 -adrenergic receptor-stimulated lipolysis and highlight BK channel inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to enhance lipolysis and combat obesity and insulin resistance.

The Ser565 site of HSL is recognized as a phosphorylation target for multiple kinases, with different kinases modulating the activity and lipolytic process of HSL through phosphorylation at this site (, ). Among these kinases, AMPK is notably highlighted as a key regulator of HSL phosphorylation at the Ser565 site. It has been suggested in previous studies that AMPK-mediated regulation of HSL phosphorylation at the Ser565 site serves as a negative regulatory mechanism (, , ). Our investigation revealed that the BK-KO did not change the phosphorylation level of the inhibitory Ser565 site of HSL ( and ). Additionally, the phosphorylation level of AMPK was also unchanged by BK-KO (). Importantly, our data corroborate these findings and further demonstrate that BK deficiency significantly enhances the phosphorylation of HSL at Ser660, while having no discernible impact on the phosphorylation of HSL at Ser565. Thus, BK deficiency-mediated acceleration of lipolysis is primarily attributable to activating phosphorylation of HSL at Ser660, distinctly independent of inhibitory phosphorylation of HSL at Ser565.

The molecular mechanisms by which BK channels regulate the cAMP/PKA/HSL signaling pathway in adipocytes remain incompletely understood. As calcium (Ca 2+ )-activated potassium (K + ) channels, BK channel activity is closely coupled to dynamic changes in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations (, ). In the present study, we demonstrated that BK channel deficiency or pharmacological inhibition significantly enhanced β3-adrenergic receptor agonist CL-316243-induced lipolysis, accompanied by transient elevations in intracellular Ca 2+ levels (). These findings suggest that BK channels may influence the activity of the cAMP/PKA/HSL signaling axis through modulating transient Ca 2+ dynamics. According to relevant published literature, there is a close and complex crosstalk between intracellular Ca 2+ and the cAMP/PKA signaling pathway. On the one hand, Ca 2+ can directly modulate the activity of various adenylyl cyclase (AC) isoforms to promote or inhibit cAMP synthesis (, ). On the other hand, Ca 2+ also influences the catalytic efficiency of phosphodiesterases (PDEs) to affect cAMP degradation (). Through these two pathways, Ca 2+ jointly alters intracellular cAMP levels, thereby regulating the activation of downstream PKA and the phosphorylation of its substrate HSL, and ultimately controlling the lipolytic process. Of note, the regulation of lipolysis by intracellular Ca 2+ is complex. Previous studies have shown that sustained elevations of intracellular Ca 2+ in adipocytes primarily promote lipid synthesis and suppress lipolysis (, ), whereas the activation of lipolysis is more critically dependent on transient, localized Ca 2+ spikes (). Consistent with these observations, our study revealed that BK channel deficiency did not induce sustained Ca 2+ elevations but rather triggered transient Ca 2+ increases upon β3-adrenergic stimulation. This spatiotemporally distinct Ca 2+ signaling pattern may represent a key mechanism underlying the pro-lipolytic effect of BK channel deficiency.

It is well known that the PI 3 K-AKT signaling pathway is a major downstream pathway of the insulin receptor, and it is a classical signaling pathway that regulates lipid deposition in adipocytes. Our previous results showed that activation of BK channels induced lipid deposition in adipocytes through the insulin/PI 3 K/AKT signaling pathway, which regulates lipid synthesis (). It has now been demonstrated that insulin inhibits lipolysis in an AKT-dependent manner (, ). Further investigation revealed that in the experimental system of CL-316243-induced lipolysis, either inhibition or activation of BK channels did not change the phosphorylation level of AKT at Ser473 (), whereas the phosphorylation level of HSL at Ser660 was correspondingly increased or decreased (). These data indicate that, while we cannot exclude the possibility that BK deficiency may affect AKT signaling in the presence of insulin, the BK channel can also directly regulate lipolysis independently of AKT signaling under insulin-free conditions in vitro. Together, these findings indicate that BK channels promote lipolysis process via a PI 3 K-AKT-independent mechanism, involving direct activation of the cAMP/PKA/HSL cascade.

In summary, the BK channel is capable of responding to changes in metabolic signals and regulating the lipolysis process, thereby affecting the metabolic homeostasis of the whole organism. In this study, we identified that BK channels regulate lipolysis through the cAMP/PKA/HSL pathway, which provides a new entry point to understand the intricate regulation of the lipolysis mechanism and lays the foundation for the subsequent elucidation of the mechanism by which BK-KO attenuates obesity and related metabolic diseases. The specific mechanisms of BK channels in the regulation of lipolysis and their potential roles in metabolic diseases need to be further explored, which will provide an important theoretical basis for the development of new treatment strategies for obesity-related metabolic diseases.

This study still has certain limitations. We only confirmed the regulatory relationship among BK channels, Ca 2+ dynamics and lipolytic signaling, but did not further verify the precise molecular interaction between Ca 2+ and the cAMP/PKA axis. Future studies will focus on exploring the detailed mechanistic crosstalk of this signaling cascade to supplement and improve the regulatory network of BK channels in adipocyte lipid metabolism.

title: Additive effects of obesity and vitamin D insufficiency on all-cause and cause-specific mortality.
abstract: Obesity and vitamin D deficiency are both considered risk factors for mortality, but the potential additive effects of vitamin D status and obesity on mortality has not been well-studied. We aimed to examine the possible additive effects of obesity and vitamin D status on all-cause and cause-specific mortality. The data from the NHANES III (1988-1994) and NHANES 2001-2014 surveys were used, and multivariate Cox regression models were performed to assess the additive effects of vitamin D status and overweight/obesity/abdominal obesity on the all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality, by stratifying Cox Hazard Ratios (HRs) across different categories of vitamin D status and body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC) categories. The models were adjusted for age, race/ethnicity, gender, educational level, family income to poverty ratio, leisure-time physical activity, smoking, and drinking. Across all BMI/WC categories, there was an additive effect of the vitamin D both insufficiency and deficiency on all mortality rates, with deficiency having much stronger effect than insufficiency. Interestingly, the effect of vitamin D deficiency overcame the effect of obesity on all mortality rates. The highest HRs for overall and cardiovascular mortality were observed among vitamin D deficient obese/abdominally obese subjects, while for cancer mortality among vitamin D deficient normal weight/non-abdominally obese subjects. In stratified analyses, regarding all-cause mortality, there was an additive effect of the vitamin D both insufficiency and deficiency in all BMI/WC categories. Regarding cardiovascular mortality, there was an additive effect of vitamin D deficiency in all BMI/WC categories, but the additive effect of vitamin D insufficiency reached significance only in normal weight subjects. Regarding cancer mortality, the effect did not reach significance among obese subjects for vitamin D deficiency, while for insufficiency, significance was reached only among non-abdominally obese subjects. Interestingly, vitamin D surplus was associated with increased risk for cancer mortality in obese subjects, but there was an inadequate number of subjects in this category to make proper judgment. In conclusion, vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency gradually increase risk for mortality across all BMI/WC categories. In our analyses, vitamin D deficiency overcame the effect of obesity on mortality rates.

sections.other:
Vitamin D, as an essential micronutrient, has pleiotropic skeletal and non-skeletal actions, including its anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, anti-oxidative, and immunomodulatory effects (). An increasing number of studies have shown that vitamin D deficiency is associated with obesity and metabolic disorders related to obesity (–). Compared with normal weight subjects, obese subjects are more likely to have vitamin D deficiency, most probably due to volumetric dilution, even though other mechanisms also could have a role (, ). Currently, hypovitaminosis D is observed at high rates, most probably because of the modern lifestyle, but some argue that this may be also due to the high global obesity prevalence (, ).

Obesity and vitamin D deficiency are now considered major public health problems worldwide (). Recent meta-analyses and systematic review studies proposed that vitamin D deficiency may be associated with mortality, including all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality (–). According to previous studies, vitamin D deficiency may be more significantly associated with cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and was also closely related to some carcinoma types (–). Low levels of circulating 25-hydroxy-vitamin D [25(OH)D] may be associated with an increased risk of CVD, especially recurrent CVD events and CVD mortality (). Meanwhile, the global prevalence of obesity is also rising, and CVD is one of the main causes of death among the obese (). Additionally, obesity or serum vitamin D level may affect the severity or mortality of some diseases. For example, some research results showed that the incidence and mortality of novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) were higher in several European countries with high latitude or high obesity prevalence (). In some specific populations, such as menopausal women, it has been shown that the relationship between vitamin D levels and mortality may differ among participants with different body mass index (BMI) or waist circumference (WC), but there was no similar conclusion in the general population (, ). These studies all implied that vitamin D or obesity not only independently have an effect on mortality, but also there may be a potential additive effect between them. However, the potential additive effect of serum vitamin D status and obesity on mortality has not been well-studied.

We aimed to examine in detail the possible additive effect of obesity and vitamin D status [assessed through serum 25(OH)D concentration] with regard to all-cause and cause-specific mortality, using the data from National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (NHANES), large scale surveys conducted in the United States ().

SS and LF: conception and design. SS, YY, XW, and DZ: data collection. SS, YY, XW, QQ, and HW: data analyses and professional drafting. SS: manuscript writing. All authors were involved in writing the manuscript and had final approval of the submitted and published versions.

The datasets presented in this study can be found in online repositories. The names of the repository/repositories and accession number(s) can be found below: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/index.htm . Data for this study NHANES subsample are available upon request.

The studies involving human participants were reviewed and approved by Institutional Review Board of the National Center of Health Statistics. The patients/participants provided their written informed consent to participate in this study.
sections.methods:
The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is a nationally representative survey administered by the National Center for Health Statistics division of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and US Department of Agriculture. The NHANES utilizes a multistage, stratified area probability sampling design to select participants representative of the US population, and combines in-person interviews and physical examinations via a mobile examination center to collect data (). NHANES was approved by the institutional review board of the National Center of Health Statistics. All participants provided written informed consent.

Data were analyzed from NHANES III (1988–1994) and NHANES 2001–2014. The average follow-up time was 11.9 years. Considering age-related reductions in lean muscle mass and subclinical disorders which may affect body weight, the analysis samples were limited to participants aged 20–79 years, without pregnancy and with complete data on BMI, WC, serum 25(OH)D concentrations and survival during follow-up ().

In the current study, we classified participants as underweight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m 2 ), normal weight (BMI = 18.5–24.9 kg/m 2 ), overweight (BMI = 25.0–29.9 kg/m 2 ), and obese (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) groups according to BMI (). Abdominal obesity was defined as WC ≥ 102 cm for men and WC ≥ 88 cm for women ().

Serum 25(OH)D concentrations are considered to be the most reliable index of vitamin D status. Serum 25(OH)D concentrations were measured by DiaSorin radioimmunoassay kit (Stillwater, MN) in the NHANES III (1988–1994) and NHANES 2001–2006, and then were determined by a standardized liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) method (). Serum [25(OH)D] data from NHANES III (1988–1994) and NHANES 2001–2006 have been converted by using regression to equivalent 25(OH)D measurements from a standardized LC-MS/MS method and we used the LC-MS/MS-equivalent data for all analyses as recommended by analytical guidelines (). According to serum25(OH)D concentrations and the US Institute of Medicine (IOM) guidelines from 2011, the vitamin D status was categorized into deficiency (<12.0 ng/mL), insufficiency (12.0–19.9 ng/mL), sufficiency (20.0–50 ng/mL) and possibly harmful (>50 ng/ml) (). Nevertheless, according to the Endocrine Society guidelines form 2011, vitamin D deficiency was defined as serum levels of 25(OH)D < 20 ng/mL, insufficiency as levels 20–30 ng/mL, while levels ≥ 30 ng/ml were characterized as the normal range (). In our study we used the more strict IOM definitions ().

Mortality related information for all causes and specific diseases was obtained by linking to the National Death Index as at December 31, 2015. Outcomes were classified using ICD-10 codes. CVD mortality codes include: ICD-10 codes I00–I09, I11, I13, I20–I51, or I60–I69, and cancer mortality codes include: ICD-10 codes C00–C97. Because the deaths due to CVD were not available on US National Death Index matched mortality dataset after December 31, 2011, we only included participants from NHANES III and NHANES 2001–2010 for CVD mortality.

In the surveys, the self-reported data were collected on age, race/ethnicity, gender, educational level, ratio of family income to poverty, leisure-time physical activity, smoking, and drinking (). Leisure-time physical activity was divided into three groups: inactive group (no leisure time physical activity), moderately active group (leisure time moderate physical activity 1–5 times per week or leisure-time vigorous physical activity 1–3 times per week), active group: more moderate or vigorous leisure time physical activity than above (). The smoking status was categorized into “never,” “former,” or “current smoker.” Never smoker was defined as smoking never or less than 100 cigarettes in life. Former smoker was defined as smoking more than 100 cigarettes in life but no smoking temporally, while current smokers were those who reported temporally smoking cigarettes “every day” or “some days” (). Diet and alcohol consumption related data were from 24-h dietary recalls (only day 1 recall was included). Drinking was grouped according to the dietary guidelines for American residents ().

For continuous and categorical variables, respectively, the analysis of variance and Pearson χ2 test were performed. In addition, the Bonferroni method post-hoc tests were made in analysis of variance, and P -value was corrected for multiple comparisons by the Bonferroni method. A post-hoc power analysis was also performed in our study and the result was satisfactory (power > 0.9). We used multiple imputation based on chained equations (MICE) to impute the missing data of covariates, but we also performed analyses with excluded all subjects who miss any of the main covariates (data presented in ).

In our study, Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to estimate the hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) for outcomes. Due to the rare number of underweight participants, we only performed descriptive statistics for them. The models were adjusted age, race/ethnicity, gender, educational level, family income to poverty ratio, leisure-time physical activity, smoking and drinking. To see the additive effects on mortality, we stratified Cox Hazard Ratios (HRs) across different categories of BMI/WC and vitamin D status. Reference groups were vitamin D sufficient, normal weight and not abdominally obese. Additionally, in supplementary multivariate models in (–) we also included as covariates dietary supplement use, polyunsaturated fatty acid intake, calcium and magnesium intake ( in ), healthy eating index (HEI) ( in ) or specific foods intake in HEI scores ( in ) (HEI-1995 for NHANES 1988–1994 and HEI-2015 for NHANES 2001–2014), since those dietary factors have been shown to interact with associations of vitamin D status with mortality (–). Considering that vitamin D status is associated with renal function, we also further adjusted our main model for kidney function, estimated by the glomerular filtration rate ( in ) (). We also repeated the main analyses after excluding the participants with missing data on any of the main covariates (age, gender, race, educational level, ratio of family income to poverty, leisure-time physical activity, smoking, and drinking). All analyses were performed using Stata software (version 16). Gpower software (version 3.1) was used for power analysis. Two-sided P < 0.05 was considered for statistical significance.
sections.results:
The baseline characteristics of the participants form NHANES III and NHANES 2001–2014 were shown in . The average follow-up time was 11.9 years. We included 40058 participants aged 20–79 who were not pregnant and had no missing data on BMI, WC, serum 25(OH)D concentrations and survival. The flow chart and the comparison of baseline characteristics between excluded and included participants can be seen in and , respectively.

Among the 40,058 participants, just 1.6% were underweight, while other BMI categories were quite equally represented. However, there were significant gender differences regarding obesity and overweight prevalence: among females, the majority were obese (37.2%), and among males, the majority were overweight (39.9%). The highest proportion of obese was among non-Hispanic Blacks (40.2%), then Mexican American (33.8%), while the highest proportion of overweight was among Mexican American (39.2%), then non-Hispanic Whites (34.0%). In total, both Mexican Americans and non-Hispanic Blacks had the highest proportion of subjects with overweight/obesity. Interestingly, regarding education and family income-poverty ratio, there was no huge difference, but regarding leisure time physical activity, smoking and alcohol consumption, the lowest proportion of obese was among physically active, current smokers and those who consumed more that 14 g alcohol per day.

Abdominal obesity was present in half of the overweight subjects and in almost all of the obese subjects (95.7%).

In total, vitamin D deficiency [serum 25(OH)D < 12 ng/mL] was present in 6.0% of subjects, while insufficiency [serum 25(OH)D 12.0–19.9 ng/mL] was present in 22.9% of subjects. Among vitamin D deficient and insufficient subjects, there was the highest proportion of obese subjects (44.7 and 39.2%, respectively), then overweight subjects (27.3 and 33.4%, respectively), which means that among vitamin D deficient and insufficient subjects, respectively, 72.0 and 72.6% were with BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 . Interestingly, in both obese and underweight subjects, the proportion of vitamin D deficiency or insufficiency was higher than in normal weight or overweight group.

First, we analyzed the association of obesity levels or vitamin D status with mortality in the total sample (, ). The results indicated that obesity, abdominal obesity, vitamin D insufficiency and vitamin D deficiency were associated with increased risk for all-cause mortality and CVD mortality. Interestingly and unexpectedly, all-cause and CVD mortality HRs for vitamin D deficiency/insufficiency were higher than HRs for obesity/abdominal obesity. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with the highest risk for all-cause and CVD mortality. Interestingly, overweight had a protective effect on all-cause mortality. Regarding cancer-mortality, only vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency were associated with the increased risk. We also provide the HRs of all included covariates for all-cause and cause-specific mortality in the models which included both vitamin D status and BMI or WC categories (, ). Results were very similar, with again much higher HRs for vitamin D status vs. obesity status regarding all-cause and CVD mortality, with vitamin D deficiency bringing the highest risk. For cancer-mortality, only vitamin D status was a significant predictor, with both insufficiency and deficiency contributing to the higher risk (but deficiency contributed more). Adjusting for obesity level negligibly changed significance for vitamin D status HRs. Regarding other covariates, only leisure-time physical activity was not associated with mortality rates. Smoking brought the highest risk for all three mortalities (, ).

Next, we performed analyses to see the additive effects of vitamin D status and obesity levels, by comparing with the risk in “normal weight, vitamin D sufficient” subjects. In the whole sample analyses, there was the highest risk of all-cause and CVD mortality in participants with both obesity and vitamin D deficiency (). It is observable that through all BMI/WC categories, with deterioration of the vitamin D status, the risk for all-cause and CVD mortality gradually increases. The highest impact of joint vitamin D deficiency and obesity/abdominal obesity was on CVD mortality. Interestingly, the impact of vitamin D deficiency much overcame the effect of obesity for all-cause and CVD mortality. Actually, for all-cause mortality, among vitamin D sufficient subjects the effect of obesity was not significant, while overweight even had a protective effect. Regarding cancer mortality, only vitamin D status was associated with the increased risk, and on the highest risk were vitamin D deficient normal weight/not-abdominally obese subjects, then vitamin D deficient overweight subjects.

We further stratified the association between vitamin D status and mortality by different BMI/WC categories, with adjustments for age, race, gender, educational level, family income to poverty ratio, leisure-time physical activity, smoking, and drinking, to see in which BMI/WC category the effect of vitamin D deficiency/insufficiency will be the highest (, and ).

In all BMI- and WC-categories, both insufficiency and deficiency of vitamin D were additional risk factors for all-cause mortality. The participants with vitamin D deficiency had the most increased risk of all-cause mortality compared with those with vitamin D sufficiency, across all categories of BMI and WC. The participants with vitamin D insufficiency had also the significantly higher risk of all-cause mortality compared with vitamin D sufficiency, but the risk was lower compared with vitamin D deficiency (, ). Across all BMI/WC categories, the risk vitamin D insufficiency/deficiency quite equally increased, but seems that highest effect was among normal weight and not abdominally obese subjects ().

For CVD mortality, our data showed that the insufficient vitamin D status was an additional risk factor only in the normal weight and non-abdominally obese subjects, while in obese and abdominally obese subjects it only approached statistical significance. In contrast, vitamin D deficiency was an additional risk factor for CVD mortality in all BMI and WC-subgroups (, and ).

Regarding cancer mortality, the additive effect of vitamin D deficiency was seen in all BMI/WC categories, except in obese subjects, while the additive effect of vitamin D insufficiency was seen only in non-abdominally obese subjects. Interestingly, there was an additive effect of vitamin D surplus (levels above 50 ng/ml) and obesity on the risk for cancer mortality (). Actually, only in obese subjects the vitamin D surplus was associated with the increased risk for cancer mortality (). This observation is interesting and requires further exploration, but due to particularly small number of subjects in that category (only 4), it is not possible to draw proper concussion.

The results of our supplementary models were consistent with the results of the presented main models (), with difference that the effect of vitamin D insufficiency on was also observed in obese and abdominally obese subjects. We also repeated analyses in the main models after excluding the participants with missing any of the main covariates, and the results were very similar, with only difference that the effect of vitamin D deficiency was no more seen in obese and abdominally-obese subjects for CVD mortality, nor was seen the effect of vitamin D surplus on cancer mortality (–).
sections.discussion:
Our study, based on a large prospective cohort, indicated that lower levels of serum vitamin D were significantly associated with higher all-cause mortality. This was consistent with some data from previous research (, ). Additionally, there was an additive effect of the vitamin D both insufficiency and deficiency on all-cause mortality in all BMI/WC categories. It is well-known that obesity is one of the main risk factors for pre-mature death, and among examined 87 risk factors for pre-mature death, high BMI was on the fifth place, according to the Global burden of disease study report from 1990–2019 (). Therefore, we expected that obesity will have much more significant impact on overall mortality, compared with vitamin D status. Nevertheless, the results from this study have shown quite the opposite: the impact of vitamin D status overcome the impact of overweight and obesity, since in our Cox regression models for overall mortality, HRs for vitamin D both insufficiency and deficiency were much higher, compared with HRs for overweight and obesity, which was an expected finding (actually, overweight had a protective effect). The explanations for the additive effects of obesity and vitamin D deficiency on overall mortality are not clear. Since CVD mortality was even more connected with additive effect of vitamin D status and obesity, it could be projected the effect on overall mortality was mostly conveyed through the effect on CVD mortality. In our study, CVD mortality represented only about one fifth of total mortality, but we did not include all surveys for assessing CVD mortality, and proportion of this mortality must be higher. Additionally, mortality of many other diseases and conditions can be associated with vitamin D status and obesity, e.g., mortality from respiratory diseases, infective diseases or some other chronic diseases, including endocrine (diabetes), neurological, kidney diseases, rheumatoid diseases, etc. (). The mechanisms of the association between vitamin D and obesity can be multiple. Not only is there a simple dilution of vitamin D by increased fat deposits and plasma volume, but also some studies have indicated that in obesity the rate of uptake up vitamin D in adipose tissue may be increased, together with the increased rate of its inactivation/catabolism and elimination, and decreased rate of synthesis and absorption (, , ). Therefore, obese participants may need more vitamin D in order to maintain adequate status of serum vitamin D (, , ). With higher sequestration of vitamin D in adipose tissue, there will be much lower bioavailability of vitamin D for many other tissues, and it is known that vitamin D has numerous physiological effects (apart from the effect on calcium and phosphorus metabolism in bones and risk for fractures), including hormonal, metabolic, anti-oxidative, anti-proliferative, anti-infective, and immuno-modulatory actions. All these mechanisms may explain the higher risk for overall mortality in participants with both obesity and vitamin D deficiency.

With respect to CVD mortality, our results showed again that there was a strong additive effect of vitamin D deficiency and obesity, since participants with both obesity and vitamin D deficiency had the highest risk for CVD mortality, compared with other categories: almost 2.1 times higher than in vitamin D sufficient normal weight subjects. In contrast, obesity alone, or vitamin D deficiency alone, had only 1.3 and 1.6 times increased risk, respectively. Interestingly and unexpectedly, the effect of overweight alone on CVD mortality was not observed. In stratified analyses, in all BMI/WC categories there was the additive effect of vitamin D deficiency, but for vitamin D insufficiency, the significant additive effect was only seen in normal weight and non-abdominally obese subjects. The possible reasons are that the effect of overweight/obesity and abdominal obesity overcomes the effect of vitamin D insufficiency on CVD mortality. Moreover, for CVD mortality we only included participants from NHANES III and NHANES 2001–2010, so the smaller number of participants probably did not allow to reach significance, even though the additive effect was still present. Additionally, there can be a cut-off level in vitamin D levels, under which an additive effect of vitamin D insufficiency on the risk for CVD mortality can be observed (). Similarly, as for the all-cause mortality, with higher sequestration of vitamin D in adipose tissue, there will be much lower bioavailability of vitamin D for other tissues, which may have adverse effects on cardiovascular system, since vitamin D was shown as potent regulator of its components, despite some controversy on the particular mechanisms and outcomes (–). Our results on the effect of vitamin D status on CVD mortality are in accordance with the data from the recent systematic review by Heat et al. (), which showed the evidence for the association in observational studies. However, the data from intervention studies did not show a significant effect, which indicates a probable confounding effect in observational studies ().

It is worth noting that in our study, we observed the effect of vitamin D both deficiency and insufficiency on increased risk for cancer mortality, but the effect of obesity was not observed. In the whole sample, the highest increased risk was seen among vitamin D deficient normal weight/not-abdominally obese participants, then overweight participants. In the stratified analyses, the effect of vitamin D insufficiency/deficiency did not reach statistical significance in some weight categories, probably due to small numbers included. Interestingly, there was an additive effect of vitamin D surplus on the increased risk for cancer mortality among obese participants, both in whole sample and stratified analyses. However, because of small number of these participants (only 4), there could not be reliable conclusions and additional studies are needed. Our data are in accordance with the results from other studies, which show that vitamin D both deficiency and surplus may be associated with the increased risk for cancer mortality (, –). Better vitamin D status was associated with reduced mortality for breast cancer, colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer and hematological malignancies (). Trials with vitamin D3 supplementation also show potential effect on reduced cancer mortality (, ). Interestingly, data show that vitamin D status was not associated with the increased risk for cancer incidence, indicating that vitamin D status might be more involved in cancer progression than initial cancerogenesis ().

The main limitation of this study is that BMI, WC, and vitamin D concentrations were assessed only at one time point, at the baseline of quite long follow-up, so both vitamin D and obesity status could change in the meantime and we do not have insight into their dynamics, making reliability of our associations questionable. This is a common limitation of the long-term cohort prospective studies having only one time point measurement of the examined modifiable risk factors. Second, vitamin D levels may vary with season (), and our data did not include the season of vitamin D measurement, as very important covariate, since relevant data were not available in NHANES III (). Moreover, we also did not include data on sunlight exposure or latitude/altitude in the analyses, but surveys indicate that despite relatively sufficient sunshine, the prevalence of vitamin D deficiency is still high in Africa, India, Australia, Asia, South America, and even the Middle East (). Additionally, work time physical activity and physical activity when commuting to work were not included when assessing physical activity level, because the related data was only available in NHANES 2001–2014. We used only one 24 h dietary recall to obtain data on dietary and alcohol intakes, which is probably not enough to adequately assese usual intakes. Even though we included multiple covariates, probably some other covariates could be also considered (e.g., existence of certain chronic diseases at baseline, medication usage, level of stress, professional, and environmental risk factors, etc.). Although we had a quite large number of included participants, for CVD mortality we had only data from NHANES III and NHANES 2001–2010, because data on CVD mortality were not available in the US National Death Index matched mortality datasets after December 31, 2011. Additionally, we used multiple imputation to deal with the missing covariates data, which may also affect the results. To avoid this issue, we repeated our analyses with omitting subjects with missing data, and results showed just a small difference, particularly in obesity subgroups. This may be because most of the excluded participants were obese, and smaller number of the participants remaining for analyses did not allow to reach statistical significance for some analyses. Finally, the data refer to average US population aged 20–79 years, the findings may not be generalizable to other populations and beyond this age range.

Our results showed that there was an additive effect of the vitamin D insufficiency/deficiency on the increased risk for all-cause and CVD mortality across all BMI/WC categories, with deficiency having much stronger effect than insufficiency. Regarding cancer mortality, vitamin D deficiency significantly increased the risk in all BMI/WC categories, except among obese subjects. The highest risk for all-cause and CVD mortality was observed among vitamin D deficient and obese/abdominally obese subjects, while for cancer mortality among vitamin D deficient and normal weight/non-abdominally obese subjects. Importantly, in our study the effect of vitamin D insufficiency overcame the effect of obesity/abdominal obesity on mortality. Maintaining sufficient serum vitamin D levels may help reduce mortality, particularly in populations at high risk. More long-term and large-scale prospective cohort studies and randomized controlled trials are required to test our findings.

title: Ketogenic Diet Prevents Obesity-Associated Pancreatic Cancer Independent of Weight Loss and Induces Pancreatic Metabolic Reprogramming.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer with poor outcomes. Obesity increases the risk of PDAC through metabolic dysregulation and inflammation. Ketogenic diet (KD) can alter metabolism and has been evaluated for its effects on tumor progression in nonobese PDAC using genetically engineered mouse models (GEMM). We hypothesized that KD may also prevent obesity-associated PDAC progression by altering body composition and cancer metabolism. Therefore, male PDAC GEMMs were subjected to diet-induced obesity (DIO) using high-fat diets or maintained on a low-fat diet (LFD) for 15 weeks. Mice were then randomized to continue the initial diets or switch to a KD or matched control diet for 6 weeks. Body weight and composition, glucose tolerance, ketone levels, pancreas histology, and tissue metabolomics were assessed. Furthermore, murine pancreas-derived organoids from DIO or LFD-fed GEMMs were treated with a ketone body and analyzed using untargeted metabolomics. In obese PDAC GEMMs, KD delayed cancer progression independent of weight loss, an effect not observed in nonobese LFD-fed mice. KD-mediated PDAC suppression was associated with enrichment of pancreatic metabolic pathways that support nonglucose energy production. Ketone-treated organoids recapitulated a subset of the KD-associated metabolic differences observed in vivo, suggesting a direct metabolic effect on cancer cells. These findings suggest potential benefits of a KD in preventing obesity-associated PDAC. The diet-cancer metabolic interactions highlight potential opportunities for dietary or metabolic interventions to prevent PDAC in high-risk obese populations.SignificanceKetogenic diet prevents pancreatic cancer progression in obese, but not in nonobese, genetically engineered mouse models and modifies pancreatic metabolic pathways, informing future dietary and therapeutic strategies for high-risk obese populations.
